result.text: ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

The paper tackles the problem of choosing layerwise sparsity for magnitude-based neural network pruning, where prior work relies on heuristics or costly hyperparameter searches and performance depends critically on per-layer sparsity allocation. Their key insight is that pruning decisions should account for each layer’s contribution to the model-level ℓ2 distortion, so weight magnitudes can be rescaled into an importance score that reflects the global impact of removing parameters. They propose LAMP (layer-adaptive magnitude-based pruning), a simple, hyperparameter-free scoring scheme that rescales magnitudes by layer-level statistics to produce layerwise sparsities for global pruning, and show empirically on image classification tasks (including weight-rewinding setups) that LAMP consistently outperforms popular baselines. The method is lightweight to compute and requires no expensive tuning while yielding better sparsity–performance tradeoffs than existing layerwise allocation strategies.

The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).

The paper addresses the slow and memory-intensive training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for large-scale scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Its key insight is that scene decomposition combined with a distributed consensus optimization—specifically using ADMM—lets multiple local 3DGS models cooperate to learn a single high-quality global model while reducing per-node load and improving convergence stability. Methodologically, DOGS splits a scene into K spatial blocks, runs K local 3DGS trainings on slave nodes that periodically enforce consensus on shared Gaussian parameters with a global model on the master via ADMM, discards the local models after training, and uses only the global model for inference; this yields over 6× faster training on large scenes while maintaining or improving rendering quality.

The paper tackles the tension in offline reinforcement learning between conservatism—necessary to avoid overestimation under distribution shift—and robustness to observation deviations (e.g., sensor noise or adversarial perturbations), which excessive conservatism can undermine. The key insight is that introducing a conservative smoothing regularizer that enforces consistency and lowered value estimates not only at dataset states but also for nearby perturbed states can simultaneously preserve safety under distribution shift and improve robustness to observation errors. Methodologically, RORL augments standard offline RL by applying regularization on both the policy and value function for states in a neighborhood around dataset states, coupled with conservative value estimation for those neighborhoods; the authors provide tighter suboptimality bounds in linear MDPs and empirically show improved benchmark performance and resilience to adversarial observation perturbations.

The paper addresses the gap between state space models (SSMs) and Transformers for language modeling by targeting efficient long-range contextualization without sacrificing short-term representational power. Its key insight is that combining an SSM sublayer—which excels at capturing long-range dependencies with subquadratic complexity—with a block-wise Transformer sublayer—which handles local, short-term interactions—yields a hybrid that leverages the strengths of both families. The authors propose the Block-State Transformer (BST), present three fully parallelizable variants that integrate SSMs and block attention, and empirically show BST outperforms comparable Transformer architectures on language modeling perplexity, generalizes to longer sequences, and achieves over an order-of-magnitude layer-level speedup versus block-recurrent baselines under model parallelism.

The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

The paper addresses the gap between the likelihoods produced by diffusion ODEs (probability flow ODEs of diffusion models) and those of leading likelihood-based generative models, aiming to improve maximum likelihood estimation for deterministic diffusion-based flows. The key insight is that reparameterizing the vector field (velocity parameterization), reducing variance during training, applying a high-order flow matching fine-tuning objective with error bounds, and using a training-free truncated-normal dequantization at evaluation can jointly close the training–evaluation gap and produce smoother, more accurate ODE trajectories. Methodologically, the authors introduce velocity parameterization and variance-reduction strategies to accelerate and stabilize training, derive an error-bounded high-order flow matching loss for finetuning the learned ODE, and propose truncated-normal dequantization for evaluation without retraining; combined, these techniques yield state-of-the-art likelihoods on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 without variational dequantization or augmentation.

The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. The authors propose three consistency-based measures computed from random generations, evaluate them across eleven models (open and closed) and nine reasoning datasets, and show these measures reduce calibration error compared to prior approaches; they also find that factors like intermediate explanations, model scale, and larger sample sizes improve calibration while instruction-tuning hinders it, and that consistency-derived confidence can even boost downstream performance, with practical guidance on picking metrics based on model traits such as instruction-tuning and RLHF exposure.

The paper examines the vulnerability of recent safety-aligned large language models to simple adaptive jailbreaking attacks, showing that even top models can be reliably coerced into violating safety constraints. Its key insight is that modest adaptivity—tailoring prompt templates to the target model, leveraging available signals like token logprobs, and restricting/random-searching over token suffixes—greatly increases jailbreak success by exploiting model- and API-specific weaknesses. Methodologically, the authors implement random-search-driven attacks that maximize target token logprobs (with multiple restarts) or use transfer and prefilling strategies when logprobs are unavailable, demonstrate 100% success across a wide range of models (including GPT-4 variants, Claude via transfer/prefill, and many open models), and apply a similar restricted-token search to find trojan strings in poisoned models, releasing code and artifacts for reproducibility.

The paper tackles improving online knowledge distillation, which traditionally transfers only class probabilities between simultaneously trained networks and thus overlooks rich spatial and intensity cues in feature maps. The key insight is that adversarial learning can transfer feature-map-level knowledge more effectively than direct alignment losses (e.g., L1) by matching feature distribution rather than forcing pixelwise correspondence. The method trains multiple networks jointly with per-network discriminators that treat the network’s own feature maps as fake and others’ as real, so each network is trained to fool its discriminator and thereby learn the feature distribution of its peers, and introduces a cyclic learning scheme to scale this to more than two networks. Experiments on classification across architectures show substantial performance gains, particularly when pairing small and large networks.

The paper tackles gloss-to-pose (G2P) translation within Sign Language Production, converting gloss sequences into continuous sign pose sequences, a task challenged by the continuous, variable-length, and spatial-temporal nature of pose data. Its key insight is to recast continuous pose generation as a discrete sequence modeling problem by learning a compact, quantized latent codebook for poses and then modeling that discrete prior with a diffusion-based denoising process suited to variable-length sequences. Methodologically, they introduce Pose-VQVAE to encode continuous pose sequences into discrete latent codes, propose G2P-DDM—a discrete denoising diffusion model that generates length-varied discrete sequences—and augment generation quality with CodeUnet to capture spatial-temporal dependencies plus a heuristic sequential clustering scheme to predict sequence lengths; combined, these components yield state-of-the-art G2P performance on a public SLP benchmark.

The paper examines whether differentiable simulators—which provide first-order gradients—actually yield better policy gradient estimates than traditional zeroth-order (likelihood-ratio) methods for long-horizon, physically realistic control tasks; it identifies the problem that system properties like stiffness and discontinuities can make first-order estimators biased or high-variance and thus worse in practice. The key insight is that exact simulator gradients are not universally superior: depending on system dynamics and noise, pure first-order estimates can suffer from structural bias or variance issues, so a hybrid that interpolates between zero- and first-order information can capture the best of both worlds. Concretely, the authors analyze bias and variance trade-offs, introduce an α-order gradient estimator parameterized by α∈[0,1] that blends zeroth- and first-order terms to adaptively exploit exact gradients when helpful and fall back to robust zeroth-order behavior otherwise, and validate the approach on numerical examples showing scenarios where traditional estimators fail and the α-estimator improves performance.

The paper addresses the vulnerability of vision large language models (VLLMs) to producing harmful outputs and being easily jailbreaked, attributing this to harmful examples in vision-language fine-tuning data and to catastrophic forgetting of prior LLM safety alignment. The key insight is that a compact, curated vision-language safe instruction dataset can restore or preserve safety alignment with little to no cost to helpfulness, and can even improve helpful behavior while dramatically reducing attack success. The authors construct VLGuard, a multi-category safe instruction-following dataset, and show that integrating it into standard fine-tuning or applying it as a lightweight post-hoc fine-tune reliably teaches VLLMs to refuse unsafe requests and substantially lowers black-box adversarial attack success rates—often to near zero—while remaining broadly applicable for testing, training, and safeguarding VLLMs.

The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently and precisely evaluating video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), where existing benchmarks are costly to build and often conflate multiple skills. Its key insight is to synthetically decouple video content from query-responses by inserting unrelated visual “needles” into diverse videos and generating rule-based queries that target specific skills, enabling scalable, controlled, and skill-specific assessment. The method, VideoNIAH, automates creation of video-query-response pairs by programmatically planting needles and applying predefined query templates to produce VNBench, a suite of retrieval, ordering, and counting tasks designed to probe temporal perception, chronological ordering, and spatio-temporal coherence across varied video lengths. Using VNBench to evaluate proprietary and open-source MLLMs, the authors reveal pronounced differences in model capabilities, analyze failure modes, and offer recommendations for improving video MLLM training.

The paper addresses protecting publicly shared data from unauthorized model training by creating “unlearnable” perturbed examples, noting that prior methods produce perturbations that fail to transfer across different training settings and datasets. Its key insight is that enhancing class-wise linear separability of perturbed data via a Classwise Separability Discriminant (CSD) objective yields perturbations whose unlearnable effects generalize better to unseen training configurations and datasets. The method generates imperceptible additive perturbations optimized to increase class separability penalties (using CSD) so that models trained on the poisoned data learn features that do not generalize, and the authors validate through extensive experiments that these CSD-based unlearnable examples transfer more effectively across varied training settings and datasets.

The paper tackles improving GAN performance by refining consistency regularization on the discriminator, addressing the problem that naive consistency constraints can introduce visual artifacts and suboptimal synthesis quality. The key insight is that careful design of the consistency loss—avoiding alignment of augmented and unaugmented discriminator outputs in ways that force the generator to produce artifacts, and modifying how augmentations, perturbation magnitudes, and loss targets are applied—yields better training signals without degrading sample fidelity. Methodologically, the authors identify failure modes of prior consistency schemes, introduce fixes and several practical modifications (including adjusted augmentation strategies, targeted consistency targets, and regularization schedules), and validate these changes across architectures and datasets to achieve state-of-the-art FID improvements on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet-2012.

The paper addresses how to adapt few-shot object detection (FSOD) to the era of large vision-language models (VLMs), noting that off-the-shelf zero-shot VLMs already outperform SOTA few-shot detectors but can misalign with target application concepts. Their key insight is that few-shot recognition should be reframed as aligning foundation models to target concepts using a small set of multi-modal exemplars (text plus images), since examples and brief instructions can define category semantics more precisely than class names alone. To operationalize this, they introduce Foundational FSOD, a benchmark and protocol that fine-tunes pre-trained VLMs on K-shot multi-modal examples per class (repurposing nuImages), evaluate several open-source VLMs, analyze method performance, and run a community competition demonstrating large gains from tailored adaptation.

The paper addresses PPO's sample inefficiency stemming from its inability to leverage off-policy data. Its key insight is that a suitably designed clipped surrogate objective can safely incorporate off-policy samples while constraining policy updates to avoid instability, yielding update distances comparable to on-policy PPO. The method derives and analyzes this off-policy clipped surrogate, proves that its policy update distance remains consistent with PPO’s stability properties, and implements an iterative policy optimization algorithm that uses past experience to improve sample efficiency. Empirical results on continuous control benchmarks show the proposed Off-Policy PPO outperforms or matches state-of-the-art baselines on most tasks.

The paper tackles inefficient coordination in multi-agent reinforcement learning by introducing emergent, interpretable roles instead of relying on hand-designed role definitions. The key insight is that letting roles emerge as learnable stochastic embeddings and conditioning individual policies on these roles encourages specialization and shared behavior among similarly-abled agents without prior domain knowledge. Methodologically, ROMA builds a role embedding space trained with two novel regularizers—one promoting identifiability of roles from behavior and another encouraging specialization by linking roles to task-specific utility—and conditions each agent’s policy on sampled role embeddings so agents with similar roles share learning and specialize on subtasks; empirical results on StarCraft II micromanagement tasks show the approach yields dynamic, identifiable roles and improved performance.

The paper tackles the problem of finding hidden input parameters that produce desired observations in generic inverse problems and argues that inverse methods should be evaluated by how solution quality improves over time rather than by a single best guess. The key insight is that many deep-learning–based inverse methods act as stochastic samplers of the solution space, so benchmarking should treat them as time-dependent search processes and that combining a learned forward model with gradient-based search can exploit this viewpoint. Methodologically, the authors introduce time-to-solution benchmarking across four tasks (two prior benchmarks, one toy visualization, and a new metamaterial design task), compare state-of-the-art inverse models under this metric, and propose the “neural-adjoint” approach which trains a neural network surrogate of the forward process and then uses backpropagation through that surrogate to iteratively optimize inputs, demonstrating superior performance in several settings.

The paper addresses the lack of standardized data and evaluation protocols for applying deep learning to computational lithography—specifically lithography simulation and inverse lithography mask optimization—which hinders practical deployment of AI-driven ILT in semiconductor manufacturing. Its key insight is that a large, diverse, and realistically generated dataset paired with consistent ground-truth simulations and an evaluation framework can accelerate model development and enable fair benchmarking across tasks. To realize this, the authors release LithoBench, a dataset of over 120k layout tiles drawn from real designs and synthesized topologies with labels produced by a well-known lithography model and an advanced ILT method, and they provide an accompanying framework to train and evaluate DNNs, demonstrating baseline performance of state-of-the-art models on simulation and mask optimization tasks.

The paper tackles the limitation of open-set and universal domain adaptation methods that lump all novel target categories into a single “unknown” class, which prevents discriminative learning for those novel categories and stops further classification of them. Its key insight is to treat novel-category discovery as a self-labeling clustering problem over the entire target set and to use self-supervised representation learning combined with a mutual-information objective so that labels and inputs become highly predictive of each other, enabling simultaneous identification of seen and unseen categories. The method trains a network on target samples with SSL to learn robust features, applies a clustering/self-labeling mechanism to assign pseudo-labels across both known and novel classes, and maximizes mutual information between these pseudo-labels and inputs to refine category assignments; experiments across multiple domain-adaptation settings show substantial gains over prior approaches.

The paper addresses the problem of detecting post-training backdoor attacks on classifiers when the defender lacks the training data or clean reference models, focusing particularly on challenging two-class settings and cases with multiple simultaneous attacks. The key insight is that reverse-engineered candidate backdoor patterns can be evaluated by an expected transferability (ET) statistic that quantifies how consistently a recovered pattern causes inputs from other classes to be misclassified to the same target, and that this ET score yields a domain- and attack-configuration–agnostic separation between attacked and clean models. The method reverse-engineers potential backdoor patterns from the deployed classifier, computes the ET statistic for these candidates (using the classifier’s responses on held-out inputs rather than any training labels), and flags models as backdoored when ET exceeds a fixed threshold; experiments on six benchmarks show the approach reliably detects both two-class and multi-attack scenarios across different reverse-engineering algorithms.

The paper addresses the limited expressiveness of Neural Processes (NPs), whose reliance on a single global latent variable hinders modeling complex, multimodal data-generating processes and restricts their applicability in meta-learning and few-shot settings. Its key insight is that augmenting NPs with a mixture-of-experts mechanism yields a richer, more flexible meta-representation by allowing multiple specialized latent components to capture diverse modes and local structure across tasks while preserving exchangeability. The method, Mixture of Expert Neural Processes (MoE-NPs), integrates a gating network and multiple expert NPs so that for each context the model infers a mixture over expert latents and aggregates expert predictions to produce task-conditional outputs; this architecture is trained end-to-end and applied to few-shot supervised and meta-reinforcement learning benchmarks, where it shows improved generalization to unseen tasks.

The paper addresses the gap in understanding why AlphaZero-style Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) heuristics work and how to improve them by framing them as optimization rather than ad-hoc rules. Its key insight is that common MCTS selection rules (including AlphaZero's PUCT and UCT) can be interpreted as approximate solutions to a specific regularized policy optimization problem, so replacing the approximation with the exact optimizer should yield better search policies. Methodologically, the authors derive the underlying regularized optimization formulation, design a variant of AlphaZero that computes the exact solution to that optimization at each node (instead of using the heuristic selection formula), and empirically demonstrate that this principled variant consistently outperforms the original AlphaZero across multiple domains.

The paper investigates how commonly used baselines in policy gradient methods affect optimization beyond merely reducing gradient variance, showing that baseline choice can change the optimization dynamics and even harm learning despite lower variance. The key insight is that baselines influence the update direction and curvature of the expected update—so two baselines with identical variance can lead to different trajectories and convergence properties, and some baselines can cause natural policy gradient to converge to suboptimal policies for any stepsize when sampling is tied to the current policy. The authors analyze simple illustrative examples and theoretical conditions, and propose decoupling the sampling policy from the current policy to restore robust convergence for a much broader set of baselines, arguing for treating stochasticity in updates more carefully than by variance reduction alone.

The paper addresses automated detection of fake news in full-length online articles paired with images, using the FakeNewsNet repository where prior work focused mainly on shorter texts or unimodal inputs. Its key insight is that transfer learning with pretrained language and vision models can capture richer semantic and contextual signals across text and images, and that fusing these multimodal representations yields better discrimination between real and fake articles than single-modality baselines. The method, SpotFake+, applies pretrained encoders to extract textual and visual features from entire articles and their associated images, transfers and fine-tunes these representations, and fuses them in a downstream classifier to predict veracity; experiments show it outperforms unimodal and prior multimodal models on the dataset, and the authors release their pretrained model for community use.

The paper addresses improving out-of-sample generalization by incorporating causal structure into neural-network regularization, motivated by evidence that predicting effects from causes yields lower test error than anti-causal learning. Its key insight is to jointly learn an input-layer-embedded adjacency matrix that represents a causal DAG and use that discovered causal graph to guide regularization, focusing reconstruction only on features with causal neighbors rather than reconstructing all inputs. The method, CASTLE, embeds a differentiable DAG adjacency matrix into the network, enforces acyclicity, and adds a reconstruction-based regularizer that reconstructs only causally connected features while training the predictor end-to-end; the authors prove a generalization bound and empirically show consistent out-of-sample improvements over standard regularizers on synthetic and real datasets.

The paper tackles how to enable frozen large language models (LLMs) to both understand and generate non-linguistic modalities (e.g., images, videos) without changing the LLM weights. The key insight is to map pixels to and from the LLM’s own lexical space via a hierarchical "semantic pyramid" of tokens that jointly encode high-level semantics and fine-grained visual detail, so the LLM can reason about and produce visual content using its native vocabulary. Methodologically, SPAE trains an encoder–decoder that converts images into sequences of interpretable lexical tokens aligned with the LLM’s vocabulary and reconstructs images from those tokens using multiscale latent representations, then uses in-context prompting with frozen PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5 to perform and evaluate multimodal understanding and generation tasks. This approach yields the first demonstration of frozen LLM image generation and substantially improves image understanding performance (over 25% relative) under the same frozen-LM setting.

The paper tackles the persistent problem of translating idiomatic, non-compositional expressions that Transformer-based MT systems and general LMs often render too literally, missing intended figurative meanings. Its key insight is that a scalable, context-aware idiom knowledge base — populated and distilled using large LMs — can supply compact, human-aligned semantic paraphrases of idioms that smaller models can reliably use at inference to produce correct translations. The method constructs a multilingual IdiomKB by extracting and normalizing idiom meanings with large LMs, stores them in a compact retrievable format, and integrates retrieval-augmented translation where models like BLOOMZ, Alpaca, and InstructGPT consult the KB to replace or guide translations; evaluation uses a novel GPT-4-powered, human-aligned metric plus human judgments to show substantial translation improvements.

The paper addresses the limited use of image information in current cross-modal 3D object detectors, which leaves LiDAR-based systems bottlenecked by sparse point clouds and underexploited visual cues. Its key insight is that an image branch can provide spatially precise, local geometry cues and also improve point-cloud feature learning via backpropagated gradients if tasks and connections are designed appropriately. The method, UPIDet, adds a 2D auxiliary task—normalized local coordinate map (NLCM) estimation—to teach images local, spatially-aware features that complement sparse points, and introduces a lightweight point-to-pixel module that links the image objectives to the point-cloud backbone so gradients from the image branch enhance point representations; extensive experiments and ablations demonstrate significant gains (including state-of-the-art cyclist performance on KITTI).

AnyText tackles the persistent problem of inaccurate or unnatural-looking text in generated images by introducing a diffusion-based system specialized for multilingual visual text generation and editing. Its key insight is to combine an auxiliary latent module that conditions on glyphs, positions, and masked images with a text embedding module that encodes stroke-aware OCR embeddings and blends them with caption tokens, enabling generated text to match both visual strokes and linguistic content. The method trains this dual-module diffusion pipeline with novel losses—text-control diffusion loss and text perceptual loss—on a newly released AnyWord-3M dataset of 3 million multilingual image–text–OCR pairs, and can be plugged into existing community diffusion models for accurate rendering or editing; evaluations on the proposed AnyText-benchmark show substantial improvements over prior approaches.

The paper tackles the problem of spurious, low-quality samples produced by GANs that lie outside the true data manifold and waste model capacity when the generator learns to reproduce them. The key insight is that removing rare or low-density instances from the training set before GAN training redirects model capacity toward high-density, perceptually relevant regions and thereby improves sample fidelity and efficiency. The method embeds dataset images into a perceptual feature space, fits a simple density model to identify low-density regions, performs instance selection by removing those outlying examples, and then trains existing GAN architectures (e.g., Self-Attention GAN, BigGAN) on the refined dataset, yielding substantially better Inception Score and FID while using fewer parameters and less training time.

The paper tackles representation learning on textual graphs, where node embeddings must capture both individual node text and neighborhood context, and points out that prevailing cascaded architectures—encoding text independently then aggregating with GNNs—fail to model interdependent semantics across nodes. The key insight is to tightly fuse text encoding and graph aggregation by nesting layerwise GNN components alongside transformer blocks so that each transformer layer receives and updates node representations informed by the evolving graph context, enabling iterative, global-aware semantic comprehension. The proposed GraphFormers architecture interleaves transformer layers with GNN layers and is trained with a progressive strategy that first uses manipulated data and then original data to strengthen graph integration; evaluations on three large benchmarks show it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with similar efficiency.

The paper tackles efficient autonomous exploration in realistic 3D environments by combining learned perception with reliable planning to avoid the high sample complexity and brittleness of end-to-end learned navigation. The key insight is that a modular, hierarchical architecture—pairing a learned SLAM-like mapping module and learned global/local policies with classical analytical path planners—lets each component exploit its strengths (flexible sensory input and structural priors from learning; precise trajectory execution from planning) while containing error propagation and training cost. The method implements an Active Neural SLAM system where a learned mapping/pose module feeds a learned global policy that proposes informative long-range goals, a learned local policy robustly executes short-horizon motion amid state-estimation noise, and an analytical planner produces collision-free paths between waypoints; this decomposition enables efficient training, strong empirical performance in realistic simulators, and easy transfer to PointGoal navigation tasks.

The paper addresses composed image retrieval with iterative text feedback, noting that users search from coarse to fine-grained descriptions but existing pairwise training focuses only on fine-grained one-to-one matches and harms recall. The key insight is to model retrieval as a multi-grained matching problem by treating coarse-grained queries as allowing larger uncertainty (fluctuations) in feature space and fine-grained queries as smaller fluctuations, so the model should not force away plausible candidates early. Methodologically, they introduce uncertainty modeling that simulates multi-grained queries via identically distributed feature perturbations and uncertainty regularization that adapts the matching objective to the fluctuation range, which preserves candidate sets during early stages and yields consistent Recall@50 improvements on FashionIQ, Fashion200k, and Shoes.

The paper tackles automated EEG-based seizure detection and classification, focusing on three gaps in prior work: modeling EEG's non-Euclidean spatiotemporal structure, improving performance on rare seizure types, and providing quantitative interpretability for seizure localization. The key insight is that graph neural networks (GNNs) can better capture electrode geometry or dynamic brain connectivity in EEGs and that self-supervised pre-training—predicting the next time period’s preprocessed signals—boosts downstream detection/classification performance and helps rare-class learning. The method builds EEG graphs (geometry- or connectivity-based), trains GNNs with a self-supervised next-step signal prediction objective before supervised fine-tuning, and introduces a quantitative interpretability metric to evaluate localization ability. Evaluated on a large public dataset, the approach outperforms prior methods on detection (AUROC 0.875) and classification (weighted F1 0.749), notably improving rare seizure classification and precise localization of focal seizures.

The paper addresses the problem of selecting activation functions that yield efficient neural network approximations of smooth functions, contrasting commonly used piecewise-linear ReLU networks with alternatives. Its key insight is that rational activation functions—ratios of polynomials—provide greater flexibility and smoothness, enabling networks to approximate smooth target functions with provably optimal complexity and substantially less depth than ReLU networks. Methodologically, the authors derive theoretical approximation bounds and complexity lower/upper bounds showing exponential depth savings for rational nets, and validate these advantages with numerical experiments comparing rational-activation networks to ReLU counterparts.

The paper tackles the problem of unreliable, overconfident uncertainty estimates in meta-learning when data are scarce, which undermines downstream decisions like Bayesian optimization. Its key insight is to model meta-learned priors as stochastic processes and perform meta-level regularization directly in function space so the meta-learner can be encouraged to exhibit high epistemic uncertainty where meta-training data are sparse. The proposed method, F-PACOH, implements this idea by learning function-space priors and applying regularization that shapes probabilistic predictions (rather than parameter posteriors), yielding better-calibrated uncertainty; the authors demonstrate integration with sequential decision-making and show strong empirical gains on meta-learning for BO compared to other meta-learners and baselines.

The paper tackles the need for faster and more accurate deep learning on 3D point clouds by revisiting and improving the Set Abstraction (SA) building block from PointNet++; its goal is to reduce computation while boosting accuracy for tasks like classification and segmentation. The key insight is that the original SA mixes channel-wise feature learning and spatial aggregation in a single step, and separating these concerns lets each be learned more efficiently—further enhanced by an Anisotropic Reduction that captures direction-dependent (anisotropic) spatial correlations. Methodologically, the authors design a Separable Set Abstraction module that first learns channel correlations and then spatial correlations, embed an Anisotropic Separable SA (ASSA) variant that uses anisotropic pooling/aggregation, replace PointNet++’s SA modules with ASSA to form ASSANet, and demonstrate via extensive experiments that this architecture yields substantially higher accuracy and much faster inference on benchmarks like S3DIS and part segmentation.

The paper tackles the limitation in tool-augmented LLM training where only successful decision-tree (inference-tree) trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning, neglecting failed explorations that could inform better tool-usage policies. Its key insight is that failed paths in expert inference trees contain actionable preference signals that, when converted into stepwise preference data and used to directly optimize the model’s policy, can expand the learning signal beyond successful trajectories and improve generalization. Methodologically, the authors construct step-wise preference pairs from both successful and failed tree branches, first SFT the LLM on successful tool-usage trajectories and then apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with the derived preference data to produce TP-LLaMA; experiments show this approach improves performance, generalization to unseen APIs, and reasoning efficiency over prior baselines like ToolLLaMA.

The paper tackles the gap between rapid systems-level advances (in compilers, networking, and hardware) and the slow uptake of those advances within large machine learning frameworks, which hampers prototyping of novel computational paradigms and systems research. Its key insight is that enabling systems researchers requires a library designed with open, modular, and easily customizable internals—alongside research-ready models—so that new ideas can be implemented and evaluated with low friction and realistic workloads. To realize this, the authors present Flashlight, an open-source ML library that emphasizes modularity and performance, offering state-of-the-art models and training setups while keeping overhead low so it competes with or outperforms mainstream frameworks. By making it simple to iterate on computational primitives and tooling, Flashlight aims to accelerate systems-driven innovation that can be adopted by larger frameworks downstream.

The paper tackles the problem of imputing missing values in tabular datasets by extending masked autoencoding to this domain. The key insight is that, beyond treating naturally missing entries as masks, intentionally re-masking a random subset of observed values during training forces the autoencoder to learn representations that are invariant to missingness and better generalize to unobserved entries. The method, called ReMasker, trains a masked autoencoder to reconstruct these re-masked values (while leaving original missing entries masked), then applies the trained model to predict the true missing entries at inference time; empirical results on benchmarks show it matches or outperforms state-of-the-art imputers, especially as missingness increases, and theoretical analysis supports its missingness-invariance property.

The paper addresses inefficiencies in current vision-language fine-tuning pipelines that convert visual encoder outputs into long visual prompt tokens for language model inputs, which bloats input length and slows training/inference. The key insight is to treat visual prompts not as input tokens but as external knowledge injected directly into the language model’s Feed-Forward Network (FFN), leveraging recent evidence that FFNs function like key-value memory where parameters can store modality-specific information. The proposed method, Memory-Space Visual Prompting (MemVP), concatenates learned visual prompt parameters with FFN weights to inject visual knowledge into the model’s internal memory space and then applies parameter-efficient fine-tuning; experiments show this approach reduces training time and inference latency while outperforming prior PEFT baselines across diverse VL tasks.

The paper addresses the problem of merging multiple finetuned model weights into a single multi-task model without suffering large performance drops or requiring additional data or training. The key insight is that no single model’s weights can simultaneously represent all task-specific solutions, so instead the authors elect a unified base model from the available weights and add extremely lightweight, task-specific modulators that adjust weight direction (via binary masks) and magnitude (via rescalers) to align each task model to the unified base. Their method, EMR-Merging, therefore consists of (a) selecting an elected model as the common backbone and (b) generating and applying per-task masks and rescalers to merge other models into that backbone; this tuning-free approach requires no extra data or training and achieves strong performance across many vision, NLP, PEFT, and multi-modal merging scenarios.

The paper tackles the problem of generating long-term musical soundtracks that are rhythmically synchronized with visual cues, addressing limitations of prior work that either use rigid, pre-defined music representations or directly generate waveforms only for short, simple scenarios with unstable quality. The key insight is to frame video-conditioned soundtrack synthesis as latent-space conditional diffusion, combined with context-aware conditioning that captures temporal structure over long horizons to improve rhythmic alignment and generative flexibility. Methodologically, the authors introduce LORIS, which uses a latent diffusion probabilistic model to synthesize waveforms and a set of temporal conditioning encoders that encode rhythmic visual context for long-term generation, and they validate the approach across extended scenarios (dance and sports) on a new benchmark with improved metrics and baselines, showing state-of-the-art musical quality and rhythmic correspondence.

ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. The authors propose three consistency-based measures computed from random generations, evaluate them across eleven models (open and closed) and nine reasoning datasets, and show these measures reduce calibration error compared to prior approaches; they also find that factors like intermediate explanations, model scale, and larger sample sizes improve calibration while instruction-tuning hinders it, and that consistency-derived confidence can even boost downstream performance, with practical guidance on picking metrics based on model traits such as instruction-tuning and RLHF exposure.

The paper examines the vulnerability of recent safety-aligned large language models to simple adaptive jailbreaking attacks, showing that even top models can be reliably coerced into violating safety constraints. Its key insight is that modest adaptivity—tailoring prompt templates to the target model, leveraging available signals like token logprobs, and restricting/random-searching over token suffixes—greatly increases jailbreak success by exploiting model- and API-specific weaknesses. Methodologically, the authors implement random-search-driven attacks that maximize target token logprobs (with multiple restarts) or use transfer and prefilling strategies when logprobs are unavailable, demonstrate 100% success across a wide range of models (including GPT-4 variants, Claude via transfer/prefill, and many open models), and apply a similar restricted-token search to find trojan strings in poisoned models, releasing code and artifacts for reproducibility.

result.text: The paper investigates how commonly used baselines in policy gradient methods affect optimization beyond merely reducing gradient variance, showing that baseline choice can change the optimization dynamics and even harm learning despite lower variance. The key insight is that baselines influence the update direction and curvature of the expected update—so two baselines with identical variance can lead to different trajectories and convergence properties, and some baselines can cause natural policy gradient to converge to suboptimal policies for any stepsize when sampling is tied to the current policy. The method embeds dataset images into a perceptual feature space, fits a simple density model to identify low-density regions, performs instance selection by removing those outlying examples, and then trains existing GAN architectures (e.g., Self-Attention GAN, BigGAN) on the refined dataset, yielding substantially better Inception Score and FID while using fewer parameters and less training time.

result.text: The paper tackles representation learning on textual graphs, where node embeddings must capture both individual node text and neighborhood context, and points out that prevailing cascaded architectures—encoding text independently then aggregating with GNNs—fail to model interdependent semantics across nodes. The key insight is to tightly fuse text encoding and graph aggregation by nesting layerwise GNN components alongside transformer blocks so that each transformer layer receives and updates node representations informed by the evolving graph context, enabling iterative, global-aware semantic comprehension. The proposed GraphFormers architecture interleaves transformer layers with GNN layers and is trained with a progressive strategy that first uses manipulated data and then original data to strengthen graph integration; evaluations on three large benchmarks show it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with similar efficiency.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient autonomous exploration in realistic 3D environments by combining learned perception with reliable planning to avoid the high sample complexity and brittleness of end-to-end learned navigation. The key insight is that a modular, hierarchical architecture—pairing a learned SLAM-like mapping module and learned global/local policies with classical analytical path planners—lets each component exploit its strengths (flexible sensory input and structural priors from learning; precise trajectory execution from planning) while containing error propagation and training cost. The method implements an Active Neural SLAM system where a learned mapping/pose module feeds a learned global policy that proposes informative long-range goals, a learned local policy robustly executes short-horizon motion amid state-estimation noise, and an analytical planner produces collision-free paths between waypoints; this decomposition enables efficient training, strong empirical performance in realistic simulators, and easy transfer to PointGoal navigation tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses composed image retrieval with iterative text feedback, noting that users search from coarse to fine-grained descriptions but existing pairwise training focuses only on fine-grained one-to-one matches and harms recall. The key insight is to model retrieval as a multi-grained matching problem by treating coarse-grained queries as allowing larger uncertainty (fluctuations) in feature space and fine-grained queries as smaller fluctuations, so the model should not force away plausible candidates early. Methodologically, they introduce uncertainty modeling that simulates multi-grained queries via identically distributed feature perturbations and uncertainty regularization that adapts the matching objective to the fluctuation range, which preserves candidate sets during early stages and yields consistent Recall@50 improvements on FashionIQ, Fashion200k, and Shoes.

result.text: The paper tackles automated EEG-based seizure detection and classification, focusing on three gaps in prior work: modeling EEG's non-Euclidean spatiotemporal structure, improving performance on rare seizure types, and providing quantitative interpretability for seizure localization. The key insight is that graph neural networks (GNNs) can better capture electrode geometry or dynamic brain connectivity in EEGs and that self-supervised pre-training—predicting the next time period’s preprocessed signals—boosts downstream detection/classification performance and helps rare-class learning. The method builds EEG graphs (geometry- or connectivity-based), trains GNNs with a self-supervised next-step signal prediction objective before supervised fine-tuning, and introduces a quantitative interpretability metric to evaluate localization ability. Evaluated on a large public dataset, the approach outperforms prior methods on detection (AUROC 0.875) and classification (weighted F1 0.749), notably improving rare seizure classification and precise localization of focal seizures.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of selecting activation functions that yield efficient neural network approximations of smooth functions, contrasting commonly used piecewise-linear ReLU networks with alternatives. Its key insight is that rational activation functions—ratios of polynomials—provide greater flexibility and smoothness, enabling networks to approximate smooth target functions with provably optimal complexity and substantially less depth than ReLU networks. Methodologically, the authors derive theoretical approximation bounds and complexity lower/upper bounds showing exponential depth savings for rational nets, and validate these advantages with numerical experiments comparing rational-activation networks to ReLU counterparts.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of unreliable, overconfident uncertainty estimates in meta-learning when data are scarce, which undermines downstream decisions like Bayesian optimization. Its key insight is to model meta-learned priors as stochastic processes and perform meta-level regularization directly in function space so the meta-learner can be encouraged to exhibit high epistemic uncertainty where meta-training data are sparse. The proposed method, F-PACOH, implements this idea by learning function-space priors and applying regularization that shapes probabilistic predictions (rather than parameter posteriors), yielding better-calibrated uncertainty; the authors demonstrate integration with sequential decision-making and show strong empirical gains on meta-learning for BO compared to other meta-learners and baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles the need for faster and more accurate deep learning on 3D point clouds by revisiting and improving the Set Abstraction (SA) building block from PointNet++; its goal is to reduce computation while boosting accuracy for tasks like classification and segmentation. The key insight is that the original SA mixes channel-wise feature learning and spatial aggregation in a single step, and separating these concerns lets each be learned more efficiently—further enhanced by an Anisotropic Reduction that captures direction-dependent (anisotropic) spatial correlations. Methodologically, the authors design a Separable Set Abstraction module that first learns channel correlations and then spatial correlations, embed an Anisotropic Separable SA (ASSA) variant that uses anisotropic pooling/aggregation, replace PointNet++’s SA modules with ASSA to form ASSANet, and demonstrate via extensive experiments that this architecture yields substantially higher accuracy and much faster inference on benchmarks like S3DIS and part segmentation.

result.text: The paper tackles the limitation in tool-augmented LLM training where only successful decision-tree (inference-tree) trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning, neglecting failed explorations that could inform better tool-usage policies. Its key insight is that failed paths in expert inference trees contain actionable preference signals that, when converted into stepwise preference data and used to directly optimize the model’s policy, can expand the learning signal beyond successful trajectories and improve generalization. Methodologically, the authors construct step-wise preference pairs from both successful and failed tree branches, first SFT the LLM on successful tool-usage trajectories and then apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with the derived preference data to produce TP-LLaMA; experiments show this approach improves performance, generalization to unseen APIs, and reasoning efficiency over prior baselines like ToolLLaMA.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between rapid systems-level advances (in compilers, networking, and hardware) and the slow uptake of those advances within large machine learning frameworks, which hampers prototyping of novel computational paradigms and systems research. Its key insight is that enabling systems researchers requires a library designed with open, modular, and easily customizable internals—alongside research-ready models—so that new ideas can be implemented and evaluated with low friction and realistic workloads. To realize this, the authors present Flashlight, an open-source ML library that emphasizes modularity and performance, offering state-of-the-art models and training setups while keeping overhead low so it competes with or outperforms mainstream frameworks. By making it simple to iterate on computational primitives and tooling, Flashlight aims to accelerate systems-driven innovation that can be adopted by larger frameworks downstream.

The paper tackles the problem of imputing missing values in tabular datasets by extending masked autoencoding to this domain. The key insight is that, beyond treating naturally missing entries as masks, intentionally re-masking a random subset of observed values during training forces the autoencoder to learn representations that are invariant to missingness and better generalize to unobserved entries. The method, called ReMasker, trains a masked autoencoder to reconstruct these re-masked values (while leaving original missing entries masked), then applies the trained model to predict the true missing entries at inference time; empirical results on benchmarks show it matches or outperforms state-of-the-art imputers, especially as missingness increases, and theoretical analysis supports its missingness-invariance property.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of merging multiple finetuned model weights into a single multi-task model without suffering large performance drops or requiring additional data or training. The key insight is that no single model’s weights can simultaneously represent all task-specific solutions, so instead the authors elect a unified base model from the available weights and add extremely lightweight, task-specific modulators that adjust weight direction (via binary masks) and magnitude (via rescalers) to align each task model to the unified base. Their method, EMR-Merging, therefore consists of (a) selecting an elected model as the common backbone and (b) generating and applying per-task masks and rescalers to merge other models into that backbone; this tuning-free approach requires no extra data or training and achieves strong performance across many vision, NLP, PEFT, and multi-modal merging scenarios.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of generating long-term musical soundtracks that are rhythmically synchronized with visual cues, addressing limitations of prior work that either use rigid, pre-defined music representations or directly generate waveforms only for short, simple scenarios with unstable quality. The key insight is to frame video-conditioned soundtrack synthesis as latent-space conditional diffusion, combined with context-aware conditioning that captures temporal structure over long horizons to improve rhythmic alignment and generative flexibility. Methodologically, the authors introduce LORIS, which uses a latent diffusion probabilistic model to synthesize waveforms and a set of temporal conditioning encoders that encode rhythmic visual context for long-term generation, and they validate the approach across extended scenarios (dance and sports) on a new benchmark with improved metrics and baselines, showing state-of-the-art musical quality and rhythmic correspondence.

result.text: The paper addresses temporal knowledge graph event forecasting, specifically the difficulty of predicting future interactions for entities lacking useful historical recurrence or periodicity. Its key insight is that future events arise from both historical dependencies and unobserved non-historical factors, so modeling and contrasting these two sources can reveal whether a query depends on past events and which candidate entities are most plausible. The proposed Contrastive Event Network (CENET) learns historical and non-historical dependency signals, uses contrastive learning on query representations to decide whether the current moment is history-driven, trains a binary classifier to produce a boolean mask over candidate entities, and applies this mask during inference to improve ranking. Evaluated on five benchmarks, CENET substantially outperforms prior methods, notably improving Hits@1 by at least 8.3% on event-based datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the limited data efficiency and expressivity of graph neural networks for predicting molecular and tensorial properties, which arises in part from using rotation-invariant representations that discard directional information. Its key insight is that enforcing rotational equivariance in message passing—so node features transform appropriately under rotations—retains essential geometric information and boosts learning efficiency and accuracy while allowing compact models. The authors introduce PaiNN, a polarizable atom interaction neural network that uses equivariant atom-wise features and equivariant message and update functions to predict scalar and tensorial quantities, demonstrating improved benchmark performance, smaller/faster models, and leveraging the learned representations to predict tensor properties and molecular spectra. Applied to spectrum simulation, PaiNN achieves 4–5 orders of magnitude speedup over electronic structure calculations while maintaining accuracy.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that traditional magnitude-based pruning poorly preserves performance when applied to pretrained models during transfer learning and fine-tuning, especially at high sparsity levels. Its key insight is that pruning decisions should be adaptive to the direction of weight updates during fine-tuning—i.e., weights that consistently move toward larger magnitude are more important than those whose movement indicates they should shrink—so a movement-based criterion better captures importance than static magnitude. The proposed method, movement pruning, deterministically computes first-order scores from accumulated weight update signs (or gradients) during fine-tuning to prune weights that move in directions implying unimportance, and it can be combined with distillation; empirically this yields much better accuracy in high-sparsity regimes for large pretrained language models, retaining strong performance down to ~3% of parameters.

result.text: The paper studies why fast single-step adversarial training with FGSM can suddenly fail—“catastrophic overfitting”—losing robustness during training, and questions whether the commonly used random initialization fixes the issue. result.text: The paper tackles the trade-off in deep ensembles between increasing member diversity (which improves ensemble performance) and preserving individual network accuracy, noting that many diversity-boosting regularizers harm single-model performance. The key insight is that useful diversity should eliminate spurious, conditionally redundant information between members’ features while preserving class-relevant shared information, formalized via conditional mutual information: members may share predictive signal but should not be able to predict each other’s features beyond what the label explains. The method, DICE, augments a classification loss with an information-bottleneck term and an adversarial conditional mutual information estimator that penalizes conditional predictability between pairs of feature extractors, thereby reducing simultaneous errors without degrading class information; this yields state-of-the-art ensemble accuracy and improved calibration, uncertainty and OOD detection (e.g., 5 DICE-trained networks match 7 independently trained ones on CIFAR-10/100).

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently solving PDE-constrained optimal control problems, where repeatedly solving expensive PDEs during control optimization limits practicality. Its key insight is to replace repeated PDE solves with a learned surrogate for the PDE solution operator, trained with special regularizers so it generalizes well and respects physical structure, thereby decoupling expensive simulation from control search. The method proceeds in two phases: Phase 1 trains an operator-learning surrogate (from data or physics-based simulations) to map controls to PDE states, and Phase 2 uses this surrogate to rapidly search for optimal controls—enabling fast inference of optimal inputs for a variety of PDEs (e.g., Poisson, Burgers) and control types without intensive online computation.

The PC-PG algorithm alternates between constructing a policy cover that ensures sufficient state-action coverage (via exploration objectives and ensemble updates) and performing policy-gradient optimization restricted to that cover, yielding polynomial sample and runtime guarantees for tabular and linear/RKHS MDPs and providing robustness results under average-case and distribution-shift approximation errors. Empirical results illustrate that PC-PG improves exploration and learning across both reward-free and reward-driven tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses multimedia fake news detection by questioning how cross-modal consistency and modality-specific features contribute to judging news fidelity. Its key insight is that treating text, image pattern, and image semantics as separate “views” that each predict news veracity and cross-modal consistency allows the model to reweight and bootstrap more informative representations for the final decision. Methodologically, the authors extract per-view representations, refine and fuse them with an improved Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (iMMoE) architecture, use each view to coarsely predict fidelity while multimodal features predict consistency, and then reweigh and iteratively bootstrap the views based on those prediction scores. result.text: This paper tackles image-goal navigation without relying on simulators, reinforcement learning, or ground-truth maps, motivated by the expense and sim-to-real gap of existing methods. The key insight is that passive video of an agent roaming through environments contains sufficient self-supervised signals to learn navigation policies without active interaction or explicit rewards. NRNS is simple, scalable, and empirically outperforms prior RL-based approaches on image-goal navigation, offering a strong baseline for future work.

result.text: The paper studies how self-supervised learning (SSL) behaves when pretraining data are class-imbalanced, showing that SSL representations are substantially more robust to long-tailed distributions than supervised ones: the drop from balanced to imbalanced pretraining is much smaller for SSL across sample sizes and particularly for out-of-domain transfer. The key insight is that SSL naturally learns richer, label-irrelevant-but-transferable features from frequent classes that help recognize rare classes downstream, whereas supervised learning focuses on label-specific features and thus suffers more under imbalance. To support this, the authors run extensive empirical comparisons, semi-synthetic experiments, and theoretical analysis in simplified settings, and they propose a re-weighted regularization method—motivated by the theory—that improves SSL representation quality on imbalanced datasets and nearly closes the performance gap with balanced pretraining.

result.text: The paper addresses the prohibitive per-decision computation cost of sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design, which prevents real-time adaptive experiments in many practical settings. Its key insight is that the sequential design problem can be amortized by learning a policy network that maps past observations to the next experimental design, so decisions during deployment require only a single forward pass. The method trains this amortized design network using newly proposed contrastive information bounds as objectives tailored to the sequential setting and a symmetry-exploiting neural architecture, and at test time the learned policy produces near-optimal adaptive designs in milliseconds, outperforming baseline strategies across several tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the relationship between Transformers and structured state-space models (SSMs), motivated by recent empirical results showing SSMs can rival Transformers for language modeling and the need for more efficient architectures. Its key insight is that Transformers, various attention mechanisms, and SSMs can be unified through decompositions of structured semiseparable matrices, revealing a state-space duality (SSD) that exposes equivalent computational primitives across these model families. Leveraging SSD, the authors derive generalized models and efficient algorithms that blend selective SSM behavior with attention-like operations, and they instantiate this as Mamba-2: a refinement of the Mamba selective SSM that implements the dual formulations to achieve 2–8× speedups while retaining competitive language-modeling performance.

The paper tackles the communication bottleneck in federated learning by asking whether the space spanned by model gradients over training is low-rank and can therefore be exploited to avoid sending full parameter updates. Observing in centralized training that gradients across epochs lie in a low-dimensional subspace with a few principal components explaining 95–99% of variance, the authors introduce Look-back Gradient Multiplier (LBGM), which recycles past gradient directions and transmits only scalar multipliers for those basis directions instead of full vectors. They analyze LBGM’s convergence to characterize the trade-off between reduced communication and potential accuracy loss, and empirically show that LBGM substantially cuts transmission costs across datasets and models while remaining compatible with and improvable by existing sparsification methods.

result.text: The paper addresses improving transfer-based adversarial attacks—crafting examples on a surrogate model that reliably fool other unseen models—by targeting regions of the loss landscape that yield examples with better cross-model generalization. The key insight is that adversarial examples located in flat local maxima (low curvature regions) transfer better, so they augment the attack objective with a gradient-norm penalty to favor flatness. Because directly computing Hessian-based curvature is costly, they approximate the regularizer with a first-order approximation that interpolates neighboring gradients via random sample-based finite differences and reduce variance by averaging gradients over multiple random samples during iterative updates. Experiments on an ImageNet-compatible benchmark show the method produces flatter adversarial regions and substantially improves transferability against both normally and adversarially trained models compared to prior attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses scalable, efficient inference of continuous-time normalizing flows that transform between any chosen base and target probability densities without the heavy cost of backpropagating through ODE solvers. The key insight is to define a time-dependent stochastic interpolant density between base and target and infer the flow’s velocity directly from its probability current, which yields a simple quadratic loss on the velocity expressed as expectations that can be estimated empirically rather than via likelihood-based ODE backpropagation. The method trains a velocity field by minimizing that quadratic objective (and optionally a path-length regularizer for near-optimal transport), then integrates the resulting ordinary differential equation to sample or evaluate densities at any time; when the base is Gaussian the same velocity gives a diffusion-model-like sampler and score estimator, but the approach generally sidesteps SDEs and achieves competitive or superior density estimation and image generation while scaling ODE-based flows to much larger resolutions.

result.text: The paper tackles open-vocabulary object detection, where traditional detectors are constrained to fixed-category vocabularies and require costly bounding-box annotations to learn novel concepts; learning from image–text pairs is appealing but hard because such pairs lack explicit object–word alignments. result.text: PointGPT tackles the challenge of pre-training high-capacity transformer models for 3D point clouds, which are unordered, sparse, and suffer from a gap between pre-training objectives and downstream tasks. The key insight is to cast point-cloud pre-training as an auto-regressive generative task over spatially ordered point patches, enabling the model to learn context-conditioned latent representations that respect local geometry and global structure. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of severe performance degradation when merging multiple single-task model checkpoints into a single multi-task model and the related storage inefficiency of keeping many task-specific checkpoints.
