args.text: State-space point-cloud models currently serialize points along fixed space-filling curves, introducing order bias, while autoregressive pretraining and MAE-style masking either depend on a chosen order or rely on heavy transformers. We propose Order-Equivariant Mamba Pretraining that trains a Mamba encoder on multi-scale patch sequences under diverse, locality-preserving traversals and optimizes a permutation language modeling objective: predict randomly masked patch tokens given arbitrary visible subsets, while enforcing cross-traversal representation consistency for the same patches. A lightweight local aggregation front-end reduces redundancy before serialization, and a contrastive cross-order regularizer aligns token embeddings across permutations to yield patch-level permutation-equivalence with linear complexity. This combines Mamba’s efficiency with bidirectional context benefits of masked modeling, aiming to outperform PointMamba/PCM and Point-MAE/M2AE baselines on classification and segmentation transfer.

We propose Proxy-Trust GFlowNets for compiler graph optimization: a hardware-in-the-loop method that learns when to trust proxy cost models and adaptively allocates scarce real-device evaluations. A GFlowNet conditioned on the computation graph samples diverse high-proxy-score schedules, while a lightweight graph-conditioned proxy-reliability head modulates the inference-time diversity/temperature and selects a small batch of candidates for hardware measurement via an information-gain criterion; the resulting measurements update a calibration layer that steers future sampling. A shared graph encoder with multi-head decoders transfers across correlated tasks (e.g., operator scheduling, device placement), enabling few-shot calibration on new graphs. Evaluated on whole-graph workloads (e.g., TpuGraphs), this approach targets higher top-1 hardware speedups under a fixed evaluation budget and better generalization to unseen graphs.

result.text: The paper addresses accuracy degradation caused by structured pruning that removes whole neurons or filters from neural networks by proposing neuron merging to compensate for the lost information. The key insight is that original layer weights can be decomposed into a new weight tensor and a small scaling matrix that reweights and combines surviving neurons so their collective outputs approximate those of the removed neurons, and when activations are ReLU the scaling can often be absorbed into the next layer to avoid runtime cost. Methodologically, the authors provide a cheap, data-free decomposition based on cosine similarity between neuron weight vectors to construct the scaling matrix and new weights, yielding a merged model that preserves original feature maps and maintains accuracy without fine-tuning. Experiments on various architectures and datasets (e.g., VGG-16 on CIFAR-10) show substantial parameter reduction with minimal accuracy loss.

args.text: Equivariant Factorized Hamiltonian Networks (EF-HNet) predict molecular Hamiltonians via a low-rank, projector-sum parameterization H ≈ sum_k s_k U_k U_k^T that enforces Hermiticity and SE(3)-equivariance by constructing the projector fields U_k in per-atom local complete frames. To keep computation light and expressive, we compute U_k with a Cartesian-tensor message passing backbone that mixes irreducible components efficiently and augments each layer with MACE-style higher-body messages, capturing many-body interactions in just 1–2 rounds. Compared to direct dense prediction (e.g., QHNet), EF-HNet reduces memory and time from O(N_AO^2) to O(r N_AO) while preserving angular-channel structure, and we regularize r adaptively with sparsity penalties tied to distance and angular momentum selection rules. We train with spectral-consistency losses (eigenvalues and density-matrix constraints) in addition to elementwise supervision; on QH9 we expect a better accuracy–speed Pareto and improved transfer across molecules and basis sets.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of efficient filter pruning for compressing convolutional neural networks without the cumbersome multi-stage training and many hyperparameters typical of prior work, and it also addresses uneven pruning needs across layers. The key insight is to learn structured sparsity directly from scratch by dynamically allocating layer-wise pruning ratios and progressively increasing a sparsity-inducing penalty so the network becomes sparse gradually rather than being forced abruptly. Methodologically, DPFPS imposes a novel structured sparsity regularizer on expected pruning parameters, uses a Taylor-series-based channel sensitivity criterion to identify pruneable channels, and solves the resulting pruning-ratio optimization with an iterative soft-thresholding (ISTA) procedure under dynamic sparsity, producing a final pruned model that requires no fine-tuning. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, e.g., compressing ResNet-101 to cut 44.97% of FLOPs while slightly improving Top-5 accuracy.

result.text: The paper addresses robustness of reinforcement learning when an adversary perturbs state observations, a realistic threat model for adversarial attacks and noisy sensing in deployed agents. The key insight is that for a fixed agent policy one can compute (and therefore learn) an optimal adversary that provably minimizes the agent’s return, and that alternatingly training the agent against such a learned adversary produces stronger robustness than prior heuristic attacks. Concretely, the authors propose an Alternating Training with Learned Adversaries (ATLA) framework that jointly and online trains a policy-gradient adversary alongside the agent following the optimal-adversary formulation, and they show both theoretically and empirically—including improvements from using history-aware (LSTM) policies inspired by SA-MDP analysis—that ATLA yields state-of-the-art robustness on continuous control benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses why the Structured State Space (S4) model—an SSM-based architecture that empirically handles very long sequences—works despite using a seemingly ad-hoc “HiPPO” initialization whose theoretical role was unclear. The key insight is a generalized HiPPO framework that interprets S4 as projecting input histories onto an orthogonal basis of exponentially-warped polynomials (specifically Legendre polynomials) and shows that different orthogonal bases (e.g., Fourier) yield different long-range behaviors, thereby explaining S4’s ability to represent long dependencies and guiding principled choices like timescale initialization. result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost of self-consistency (SC) decoding for chain-of-thought multi-step reasoning, which boosts accuracy by aggregating many sampled reasoning traces but requires expensive, fixed-size sampling. The key insight is that SC’s consensus often emerges long before the preset number of samples, so dynamically stopping sampling once the answer distribution stabilizes preserves accuracy while cutting cost. They propose Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), a simple scalable procedure that monitors sampled outputs and halts further sampling when a confidence or stability criterion is met, plus a control scheme to trade off performance and cost per task/model. Empirical evaluation across arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic benchmarks with diverse model scales shows ESC dramatically reduces average sample counts (e.g., GSM8K -80.1%, MATH -33.8%) while maintaining comparable reasoning performance.

The key insight is to approximate human perceptual similarity with a neural perceptual distance (LPIPS) and define a neural perceptual threat model that bounds perturbations by this learned distance, which correlates well with human judgments. Methodologically, the authors design two perceptual adversarial attacks that search for LPIPS-bounded adversarial examples and introduce Perceptual Adversarial Training (PAT), which trains models against these perceptual attacks; empirically PAT yields robustness on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 across a wide range of 12 attack types, generalizing nearly as well as specialized adversarial training for each specific perturbation.

result.text: The paper addresses improving adversarial robustness of deep neural networks by explicitly optimizing the information bottleneck (IB) principle during model training. The key insight is that robustness can be enhanced by simultaneously increasing mutual information between latent features and labels while decreasing mutual information between inputs and latent representations, and that a robust pre-trained teacher can provide targeted guidance to achieve both. The method, called Information Bottleneck Distillation, implements two complementary distillation strategies from a robust teacher: robust soft-label distillation to boost feature–label mutual information, and adaptive feature distillation that selectively transfers teacher features to reduce input–latent mutual information; experiments against PGD and AutoAttack show substantial robustness gains.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of generating full-image co-speech gesture videos directly from speech audio—moving beyond prior work that maps audio to skeletal keypoints—to create realistic, synchronized speaker gesture sequences. The key insight is that co-speech gestures decompose into reusable, common motion patterns plus subtle, rhythmic prosodic details, so a good system should capture both coarse pattern reuse and fine-grained dynamics. To this end the authors propose ANGIE, which learns an unsupervised motion representation rather than relying on explicit body priors: a VQ-Motion Extractor compresses recurring gesture motions into a codebook of motion tokens, and a Co-Speech GPT with motion refinement predicts and refines token sequences to produce temporally coherent, prosody-aligned motion that a generator turns into high-fidelity image sequences.

args.text: Introduce Aug-EquiGrad: a discriminator regularizer that enforces augmentation-equivariant input gradients while narrowing the real–fake gradient-norm gap. For a random differentiable augmentation T used in GAN training, we penalize the mismatch between ∇x D(T(x)) and the appropriately transformed ∇x D(x) (via T’s Jacobian), and concurrently add a DigGAN-style term that reduces the norm discrepancy between ∇x D on real and generated samples; augmentation strength/probability can follow ADA and use differentiable transforms as in DiffAugment. Unlike output-consistency that can bias the generator toward artifacts, constraining the discriminator’s gradient field preserves decision boundaries while promoting smooth, transformation-consistent signals. We hypothesize this yields stronger augmentation tolerance, greater stability in limited-data regimes, and improved FID/precision-recall across CIFAR-10/FFHQ/ImageNet.

We propose Exemplar-Conditioned Open-Vocabulary Detection: a no-finetuning, in-context detector that aligns a frozen VLM to new categories using a few multimodal exemplars (images with boxes and brief descriptions). For each category, we fuse exemplar region embeddings with LLM-augmented attribute descriptors to form exemplar–text prototypes that initialize DETR-style queries which cross-attend to the target image, while an image-level VLM prior gates which prototypes to activate. This prototype-driven decoding emphasizes fine-grained cues and relations over names alone, enabling rapid adaptation to novel, fine-grained, and long-tail classes under domain shift. Compared to text-only OVD or K-shot finetuning, this design promises stronger localization and calibration from the first shot by unifying exemplar visuals, descriptive language, and scene priors without gradient updates.

result.text: We propose Support-Projected Off-Policy Mirror PPO (SPOM-PPO), a policy optimization method that safely reuses replay by combining an off-policy PPO surrogate with mirror-descent trust-region updates implemented as differentiable projection layers and an explicit behavior-support constraint. At each iteration, we optimize a CPI-style surrogate on mixed on/off-policy data while (i) projecting Gaussian policy parameters per state to a KL-bounded trust region, (ii) filtering or projecting actions outside the dataset’s estimated support, and (iii) replacing hard clipping with a smooth sigmoid window to preserve gradient signal beyond the clip range. This jointly enforces bounded update distance and avoids out-of-distribution actions even with heavy replay, enabling CPI/MDPO-like improvement guarantees where off-policy estimation error enters only in higher-order terms. Empirically, SPOM-PPO should retain PPO’s stability while achieving substantial replay-driven sample-efficiency gains on continuous-control benchmarks.

The key insight is to learn dynamic subtask assignments so agents with similar abilities are grouped to share specialized learning for a subtask while maintaining diversity across subtasks, improving collaboration and scalability. args.text: I propose score–adjoint posterior sampling for PDE-constrained inverse design: learn a diffusion prior over feasible parameter fields or a latent code, pair it with a neural-operator surrogate of the forward PDE, and run preconditioned Langevin dynamics whose drift combines the prior score with adjoint gradients of the surrogate likelihood. Use the surrogate’s Gauss–Newton metric as a Riemannian preconditioner and an active error-control loop that occasionally triggers high-fidelity PDE solves where surrogate gradient uncertainty or disagreement is high, refining the operator online. This unifies generative, sampling-based recovery with neural-adjoint search, improving time-to-solution by rapidly exploring high-probability regions while maintaining physics consistency and yielding calibrated uncertainty over designs. We will benchmark under time-to-solution across fluid/FSI and metamaterial tasks, comparing to pure diffusion-PDE samplers and pure neural-adjoint optimizers.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of existing neural operators—particularly Fourier neural operators (FNOs)—which perform global convolutions that can over-smooth and miss local features, while CNNs capture locality but are tied to a single resolution. The key insight is that by designing locally supported kernels and appropriate scalings, one can realize both differential operators (via stencil-inspired scaling of CNN kernels) and integral operators (via basis representations using discrete–continuous convolutions), thereby combining locality with the resolution-agnostic property of operator learning. The method implements localized differential and integral operator layers that plug into operator-learning architectures (e.g., augmenting FNOs) and proves the connection between CNN kernel scaling and differential operators, while constructing local integral kernels through suitable basis expansions; empirically, adding these layers to FNOs substantially reduces relative L2 error (34–72%) on challenging PDE benchmarks like turbulent 2D Navier–Stokes and spherical shallow water equations.

result.text: The paper addresses Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), where a model must recognize both known classes from labeled data and novel classes within unlabeled data, and identifies that existing methods couple learning of known and novel categories which harms generalization and prevents explicit transfer of category-specific knowledge. The key insight is to decouple the treatment of known and novel categories while explicitly aligning prototypes of known classes across labeled and unlabeled domains, enabling targeted training objectives for each group and preserving high-level semantic information. The proposed Decoupled Prototypical Network (DPN) formulates prototype alignment as a bipartite matching problem to pair known-class prototypes between datasets, and introduces Semantic-aware Prototypical Learning (SPL) that uses semantic-weighted soft assignments to produce discriminative features and reduce noisy hard pseudo-labels for both known and novel categories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this decoupled, prototype-aligned approach substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks.

args.text: Most post-training backdoor detectors assume a reusable pixel-space trigger, but input-aware and on-demand target generators evade such tests; we propose Backdoor Subspace Consistency (BSC), which seeks target-specific linear subspaces that capture the shared mechanism of many distinct per-input triggers. For a set of inputs and hypothesized targets, we reverse-engineer minimal triggering perturbations, perform robust low-rank subspace recovery across inputs to estimate a small basis per target, and then compute an Expected Subspace Transferability (EST) score by projecting held-out clean inputs onto these bases and measuring how consistently the projections alone induce the same target misclassification (no labels required). To denoise optimization artifacts and resist benign spurious features, we weight samples by feature-consistency-under-transformations during subspace estimation and optionally use UMD-style class-pair preselection to focus computation. High EST for any recovered subspace flags backdoored models in binary, X2X, and generator-based settings where no single reusable trigger exists.

result.text: The paper tackles how to train large sparsely-activated mixture-of-experts (MoE) models to handle multimodal (image and text) contrastive learning, addressing instability and uneven expert use that arise when mixing modalities in a single backbone. The key insight is that MoE layers naturally allow different experts to specialize on different modalities or subregions of the joint modality space, but require an entropy-based regularizer to stabilize training and encourage balanced expert utilization. The method, LIMoE, feeds images and text into a shared sparse MoE encoder trained with a contrastive loss and an entropy regularization term to prevent expert collapse; this design yields better compute–performance trade-offs than dense models and produces emergent modality-specific experts and improved zero-shot ImageNet accuracy competitive with larger per-modality architectures.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in understanding why AlphaZero-style Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) heuristics work and how to improve them by framing them as optimization rather than ad-hoc rules. Its key insight is that common MCTS selection rules (including AlphaZero's PUCT and UCT) can be interpreted as approximate solutions to a specific regularized policy optimization problem, so replacing the approximation with the exact optimizer should yield better search policies. Methodologically, the authors derive the underlying regularized optimization formulation, design a variant of AlphaZero that computes the exact solution to that optimization at each node (instead of using the heuristic selection formula), and empirically demonstrate that this principled variant consistently outperforms the original AlphaZero across multiple domains.

result.text: We propose Baseline-Matched Sampling (BMS) for policy-gradient RL: decouple data collection from the current policy and actively choose a replay-weighted sampling mixture that cancels baseline-induced bias in the expected natural-gradient direction. Concretely, at each iteration we jointly learn a state-value baseline and sampling-mixture weights by enforcing orthogonality of the control-variate term to the policy score under the target policy, implemented via a three-way doubly robust off-policy gradient estimator with truncated importance weights for stability; the sampling mixture is maintained by a replay-aware entropy-regularized objective. This aligns the estimated update with the intended NPG direction even when baselines alter curvature, yielding on softmax policies O(1/t) convergence as in baseline-stabilized NPG and recovering linear rates with entropy regularization, while empirically improving robustness across baseline choices without extra tuning. The design operationalizes prior insights that baselines shape optimization dynamics and that decoupling sampling restores convergence, while leveraging sample-aware entropy and minimax-optimal off-policy gradient estimation to make the decoupling practical and stable.

args.text: Passive Social Affordance Neural SLAM (PSA-NSLAM) combines offline pretraining on roaming, human-populated egocentric videos with a modular Active-Neural-SLAM-style stack to achieve human-aware navigation without simulators or RL. From video, we learn (i) a social affordance predictor that outputs time-varying traversability/cost fields and (ii) progress/relocalization estimators for image-goal conditioning, which are plugged into online geometric-semantic mapping and an analytical planner. A global policy proposes subgoals that trade off exploration/goal progress with predicted social compliance, while a local controller tracks short-horizon waypoints using the learned cost fields to anticipate and yield to moving people. Evaluated on HA3D-like dynamic benchmarks, this offline-trained, planner-grounded approach targets improved safety, success, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

The method, ChatIR, uses an LLM to produce follow-up questions from an initial image description, engages the user in multiple dialogue rounds to collect answers, and combines these dialog-enriched queries with retrieval models evaluated on a large 50K-image corpus; experiments and comparisons (including RL-trained baselines and human-questioning) show marked gains—78% success after five rounds versus 64% for single-shot retrieval.

We pretrain with a multi-scale masked modeling scheme that applies pyramid masking and a locally constrained Mamba decoder that allocates capacity to information-dense unmasked groups while reconstructing masked ones via cross-scale skips. result.text: We propose Value-Weighted Tree Preference Optimization (VW-TPO) for tool-augmented LLMs: mine both successful and failed branches of inference/action trees, but attach a learned step-value to every node via an LLM-guided value model inside an MCTS-style explorer. At each decision point, form preference pairs between taken and counterfactual sibling actions and weight them by the predicted downstream value gap, then train with DPO using a depth- and batch-adaptive beta that emphasizes high-regret, informative pairs while filtering noisy failures. By unifying tree-based self-evaluation with adaptive preference optimization, VW-TPO expands the learning signal beyond success trajectories, improves generalization to unseen tools, and reduces over-regularization and token cost via one-shot plan sampling.

result.text: The paper addresses few-shot temporal knowledge graph reasoning: predicting future facts for newly emerging entities in evolving temporal knowledge graphs where only very limited historical observations exist and distributions may shift over time. The key insight is that rigid, one-size-fits-all neighbor sampling and aggregation fails under both data scarcity and temporal drift, so the model should learn to dynamically adapt how it selects and pools recent contextual facts for each new entity using feedback from future facts. args.text: We propose a basis-covariant, SE(3)-equivariant operator predictor for molecular Hamiltonians that learns a continuous kernel H(r, r') via lightweight equivariant message passing and projects it into any atomic-orbital basis, guaranteeing Hermiticity and unitary-basis covariance. The kernel is parameterized as a low-rank sum of separable, symmetry-adapted components with locality-aware sparsification, combining QHNet-style efficient equivariant circuitry with neural-field ideas for wavefunctions to exploit nearsightedness and avoid costly high-rank tensor products. Training uses QH9 Hamiltonians with multiple randomized sub-bases per geometry to enforce basis-agnostic consistency and improve transfer across basis sets and molecular families. The result is a single model that outputs consistent Hamiltonians at different resolutions and supports downstream SCF warm starts and basis-adaptive simulations.

result.text: Develop an amortized Fisher-information streaming active learner that replaces per-batch BAIT optimization with a learned recurrent acquisition policy trained to approximate the Fisher-bound objective under streaming constraints. The policy ingests micro-batch features (uncertainty signals, Jacobian sketches for Fisher surrogates) and a compact coreset state, and outputs which points to query to meet a target rate, while a diversity controller maintains coverage via fast submodular-style updates. We train the policy offline with logged streams using contrastive information bounds as a differentiable surrogate for BAIT’s MLE error bound, and online it adapts to distribution drift via lightweight state updates. This yields BAIT-level selection quality with orders-of-magnitude lower compute and practicality in on-the-fly settings, combining amortized design, streaming AL scheduling, and scalable diversification.

result.text: Federated EF-Subspace: leverage the empirical low-rank structure of gradients to design a contractive, curvature-aware compressor within the EF-BV framework. The server maintains a streaming PCA dictionary learned from tiny client-side sketches; each client projects its gradient onto the shared r-dimensional subspace and transmits only coefficients while error feedback tracks and corrects the residual, optionally augmenting with a small client-specific subspace to handle heterogeneity. Under a spiked covariance model where the top-r components capture 1−δ of gradient energy across clients, the induced compressor’s contraction factor scales with δ, so EF-BV yields linear convergence with tighter constants than top-k/random-k and communication that is O(r) per round. This unifies subspace reuse and error-feedback, aiming to outperform LBGM and classical sparsifiers in both theory and practice.

args.text: We propose Dual-Space Curvature-Controlled Fast Adversarial Training (DS-CCFAT): combine N-FGSM-style noise+no-clip single-step input perturbations with a concurrent GSAM weight-space sharpness minimization step, leveraging the SAM–robustness link to flatten the loss and diversify adversarial directions that otherwise cause boundary concentration and catastrophic overfitting. A lightweight curvature monitor (e.g., GSAM’s surrogate gap or gradient-norm variance) drives an adaptive schedule that escalates epsilon and tunes noise/step sizes over training, reflecting evidence that higher-quality inner solves are needed later. To further regularize local linearity, we include occasional non-maximal/ diversified FGSM steps and a mild gradient-alignment penalty on a subset of batches. This one-step procedure is designed to prevent catastrophic overfitting even at large radii and approach PGD-AT robustness at roughly 1.5× the cost of FGSM-AT.

We propose Multicalibrated Conformal Consistency (MC2) for black-box LLMs: treat agreement among stochastic generations as a conformity score, and learn group-conditional stopping thresholds with split conformal calibration so that, for each discovered prompt–context subgroup, the probability that the consensus-selected answer is wrong is below a target level. Groups are induced by embedding-space clustering and LLM self-annotation signals, and an early-stopping controller halts sampling once the subgroup’s calibrated consensus threshold is crossed, otherwise abstaining when a budget is exhausted. Unlike global self-consistency or ad hoc confidence heuristics, MC2 provides finite-sample coverage guarantees at fine granularity while substantially reducing average samples by concentrating effort only where calibration requires it. We expect improved subgroup ECE/ACE and smaller candidate sets versus prior consistency-based and conformal LM methods, without white-box access.

I propose Tokenization-Diversified Smoothing (TDS), a defense that disrupts modern jailbreaks’ reliance on precise subword boundaries by randomizing tokenization at both training and inference. We adversarially optimize a lightweight safety gate (and optionally a guard prefix) against ensembles of attackers—including suffix random-search, continuous token-trigger optimization, and LLM-guided tree search—while sampling alternative BPE vocabularies and segmentation-dropout; at test time, we require agreement across multiple randomized tokenization views before allowing a continuation. This makes discrete triggers and logprob-guided searches brittle and enables randomized-smoothing-style guarantees over a bounded class of suffix manipulations, while composing naturally with prompt-based defenses. We evaluate TDS against ADC, TAP, adaptive random-search, and few-shot jailbreaks under the standardized, defense-aware settings of JailTrickBench, reporting attack success, utility, and overhead.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of identifying which intermediate feature representations from a pretrained teacher network should be used to guide a student network during knowledge distillation, noting that manually predefined links are often ineffective. Its key insight is to replace manual link selection with an attention-based meta network that learns relative similarities between all teacher and student feature levels and uses those learned similarities to weight distillation strength across every possible feature pair. The method feeds features from all levels into the meta attention module to predict pairwise similarity scores, applies those scores as distillation intensities to match teacher and student features, and trains the student with this soft, learned matching which yields more effective, efficient distillation for model compression and transfer learning.

result.text: The paper tackles derivative-free optimization in high-dimensional spaces where only function evaluations are available and traditional methods suffer from sample complexity that scales with ambient dimensionality. The key insight is that many real-world problems effectively lie on much lower-dimensional manifolds that can be modeled by learned deep nonlinear embeddings, so jointly learning the manifold structure while optimizing can decouple sample complexity from the ambient dimension. They propose an online learning algorithm that interleaves manifold learning and guided random search: at each step a learned low-dimensional representation is updated from observed function evaluations and used to generate search directions and candidates for evaluation, with theoretical analysis showing reduced sample complexity and empirical results on continuous optimization and control tasks demonstrating large gains over Augmented Random Search and other derivative-free methods.

The key insight is that training a Video-LLM on large-scale, segment-level instruction data enables fine-grained temporal reasoning and grounding rather than just global video understanding. To realize this, the authors build an automatic data-generation engine to create Moment-10M, a massive dataset of videos paired with segment-level instructions, and train Momentor on this data so it can reason about, locate, and answer questions about precise moments in videos; zero-shot evaluations show strong performance on temporally grounded comprehension and localization tasks.

args.text: We propose Subspace-Shattering Unlearnable Examples (SSUE), a defense that meta-optimizes per-example perturbations so the informative signal is dispersed into different low-dimensional subspaces across data augmentations and training checkpoints, breaking the fixed-subspace assumption exploited by simple linear purification (e.g., orthogonal projection). Concretely, SSUE keys an augmentation-aware perturbation schedule to each sample ID, uses a self-ensemble-over-checkpoints objective to enforce cross-time inconsistency of useful features, and couples classwise geometry regularization so poisoned representations remain class-consistent yet misaligned across views. To maximize transfer, the loss jointly poisons multiple pretext objectives (contrastive, BYOL/SimSiam-style predictive, and masked reconstruction) so that both supervised and self-supervised pipelines inherit the shattered subspaces. We hypothesize SSUE will outperform CSD- and SEM-style noise and SEP under adversarial training and approximate unlearning, while resisting linear and reconstruction-based purification by design, and validate on CIFAR/ImageNet and CL benchmarks with stress tests against known purification and unlearning procedures.

We propose augmentation-equivariant Jacobian consistency for GAN discriminators: instead of matching logits across views (which can induce artifacts), we align the discriminator’s input-gradient fields before and after an augmentation by penalizing ||∇x D(Tx) − JT(x)^{-T} ∇x D(x)|| on real images. The regularizer is teacher–student: a slow EMA teacher provides the target gradients to prevent the generator from exploiting the constraint, and its strength is adaptively scheduled using the real–fake gradient-gap to avoid over-regularization when the discriminator is still learning. We pair this with spectral/bidirectional spectral normalization to stabilize gradient estimation, and plug into ADA/DiffAugment pipelines without altering the adversarial loss. This Jacobian-level, augmentation-aware consistency reduces logit-level alignment pathologies while directly controlling discriminator sensitivity, yielding improved stability and fidelity in limited-data regimes.

result.text: This paper examines the common MARL practices of value decomposition and parameter sharing, showing they can fail in environments with highly multi-modal reward landscapes by biasing learning toward suboptimal, homogenized behaviors. The key insight is that while CTDE approaches with shared, decomposed Q-functions are efficient, they can provably get stuck where individualized policies found by policy-gradient (PG) methods can converge to optimal, diverse solutions. The authors provide theoretical analysis demonstrating these failure modes and convergence guarantees for independent PG, derive practical implementation recommendations for multi-agent PG to favor high rewards or diverse behaviors, and empirically validate the claims on matrix and grid games as well as StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge and Google Research Football.

args.text: We propose an anytime, budget-aware inverse design framework that tightly interleaves neural-operator learning with neural-adjoint optimization, choosing at each step whether to optimize through the surrogate or to spend compute refining it. Concretely, an ensemble neural operator (e.g., FNO or hybrid GNN+coarse solver) provides gradients and an uncertainty estimate; a controller schedules either (i) a surrogate-based gradient step when predicted improvement per unit time is high and uncertainty low, or (ii) an active high-fidelity PDE query at designs selected to maximally reduce local surrogate error, followed by rapid incremental operator updates. The loop includes lightweight physics-residual checks and gradient-disagreement tests to trigger active refinement, yielding calibrated gradients over long horizons and improved time-to-solution versus pure two-phase or purely sampling-based methods. We evaluate on PDE-constrained control and fluid-structure inverse design, showing faster convergence under fixed wall-clock budgets and better final designs by focusing surrogate capacity on the optimizer’s visited manifold.

result.text: The paper tackles high-quality image synthesis by introducing diffusion probabilistic models, a class of latent-variable generative models that iteratively corrupt and then learn to reverse a diffusion (noising) process. The key insight is a novel connection between these diffusion models and denoising score matching with Langevin dynamics, which motivates training on a specially weighted variational bound that both stabilizes learning and yields high-fidelity samples. Methodologically, they train a neural network to predict the reverse diffusion transitions (denoising steps) across many noise levels, enabling progressive, lossy decompression-style sampling that generalizes autoregressive decoding, and demonstrate state-of-the-art or competitive results on CIFAR-10 and high-resolution LSUN datasets.

args.text: We propose Backdoor Controllability Spectroscopy (BCS), an unlabeled detection method designed to catch input-aware and multi-target backdoors. For each candidate target logit, BCS learns across many unlabeled inputs and augmentations a small low-rank basis of spatially sparse perturbations that maximally increases that target, allocating optimization effort via a K-arm schedule; it then scores models by the controllability concentration (variance explained by top singular vectors of target-logit responses) and the stability of this subspace under input transformations. Backdoored models exhibit abnormally low-rank, transformation-stable controllability toward their backdoor target(s) with strong cross-target asymmetry, whereas clean models require diverse, input-specific directions; aggregating these cues yields an anomaly detector covering binary, X2X, and multi-attack cases. This reframes expected transferability from trigger instances to subspace-level controllability and complements pairwise-transfer detectors by remaining effective even when triggers are input-aware and nonreusable.

result.text: The paper addresses learning stochastic fields—random functions that produce spatially structured outputs like vector fields or images—under transformations such as rotations and reflections, highlighting that models must be equivariant to respect spatial symmetries. The key insight is that spatial invariance of the underlying stochastic field implies that the inference model must transform equivariantly, and that enforcing equivariance both characterizes allowable Gaussian process priors and yields more data-efficient, generalizable neural models. Methodologically, the authors fully characterize equivariant Gaussian processes and introduce Steerable Conditional Neural Processes (SteerCNPs), a new steerable Neural Process architecture that builds equivariance into its encoder and decoder, and demonstrate on synthetic GP vector fields, images, and weather data that SteerCNPs outperform prior models and improve transfer learning.

result.text: The paper addresses the limits of constraint-based causal discovery under the usual i.i.d. assumption—specifically that conditional independence tests can only recover causal graphs up to Markov equivalence—and asks whether richer distributional assumptions can enable full causal identification. result.text: The paper addresses the inefficiency and limited cross-layer visual interaction of current large multimodal models (LMMs) that append all visual tokens to the LLM input, which raises computation and memory costs and hampers modeling of fine-grained visual relations. The key insight is that splitting visual tokens into N groups and injecting each group into its aligned transformer layer from bottom to top—rather than dumping all tokens into the first layer—enables rich inter-token interactions across layers with minimal extra cost. The proposed DeepStack architecture applies this stacked token injection to both language and vision transformers, training models that achieve substantial gains (e.g., +2.7 and +2.9 average across nine benchmarks for 7B and 13B models) and much better performance on high-resolution tasks while using shorter visual context lengths. Empirical results show DeepStack rivals or outperforms conventional full-context LMMs and consistently improves accuracy when integrated into existing systems like LLaVA.

result.text: Passive Social Affordance Neural SLAM (PSA-NSLAM) combines offline pretraining on roaming, human-populated egocentric videos with a modular Active-Neural-SLAM-style stack to achieve human-aware navigation without simulators or RL. result.text: The paper addresses unreliable predictions in cross-modal retrieval caused by aleatoric uncertainty from low-quality or ambiguous data (e.g., corrupted images, fast videos, vague text). result.text: The paper addresses the gap that standard Bayesian optimization (BO) cannot incorporate a practitioner's prior beliefs about where the optimum lies, which wastes useful information in hyperparameter optimization and other black-box tuning tasks. The key insight is that acquisition functions can be augmented by multiplying them with a user-provided probability density over the input space (a prior belief π), thereby biasing search toward regions the user considers promising while retaining BO’s principled exploration–exploitation tradeoff. The authors introduce πBO, a simple, library-friendly modification that applies this reweighting to many common acquisition functions (analytically studying Expected Improvement), prove regret bounds and convergence rates that hold regardless of the prior, and empirically demonstrate improved performance across benchmarks— including a 12.5× time-to-accuracy speedup on a deep learning task—versus competing methods.

args.text: We propose Conformal Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (CESS), a black-box, distribution-free procedure that turns self-consistency sampling into a risk-controlled stopping rule with finite-sample guarantees. On a calibration set, we run deep self-consistency to learn a mapping from the trajectory of vote-share (and simple diversity features) to correctness, then derive nondecreasing stopping boundaries via conformal calibration so that when the live vote-trajectory crosses the boundary we stop and output the modal answer with 1−α coverage; if the boundary is not reached within a budget, we abstain. At test time, CESS sequentially samples and halts as soon as the conformal boundary is crossed, typically far earlier than fixed-size SC while guaranteeing target coverage; optional extensions produce top-K candidate sets with set-level coverage or integrate rejection tests for component-level correctness. This unifies consistency-based confidence, ESC-style cost savings, and conformal output guarantees for LMs using only black-box access.

args.text: We propose Conditional Adversarial Layer‑Mixture Distillation (CALMD) for online knowledge distillation, addressing instability from direct feature matching and semantic mismatch between teacher and student layers. CALMD builds a high‑capacity, temporally stabilized online teacher by aggregating peer features/logits, then learns an attention‑weighted mixture over the teacher’s layers for each student layer; class‑conditioned discriminators train student layers to match the distribution of these mixture targets rather than their pixels. At the output, we add a relational consistency loss that aligns inter‑class and instance‑aware correlations, and a conditional mutual‑information regularizer that suppresses peer‑specific, label‑irrelevant predictability to retain useful ensemble diversity while sharing signal. This hybrid yields stable, semantically calibrated, and relation‑preserving online distillation that is robust when peers or teachers are much stronger than the student.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that end-to-end sign language recognition and translation models often rely solely on RGB video input, which contains substantial visual redundancy and can obscure crucial articulatory cues like handshape and body movement. Its key insight is that explicitly incorporating keypoint-based skeletal information alongside raw RGB frames lets the model focus on linguistically relevant motions while still leveraging visual context, and that careful interaction between these modalities improves representation learning. Methodologically, they propose TwoStream-SLR—a dual-stream encoder that processes RGB and off-the-shelf keypoint sequences in parallel and fuses them via bidirectional lateral connections, a sign pyramid network with auxiliary supervision, and frame-level self-distillation—and extend it to translation (TwoStream-SLT) by adding a translation network on top. The combined approach yields state-of-the-art results on multiple SLR and SLT benchmarks (Phoenix-2014, Phoenix-2014T, CSL-Daily).

args.text: We propose Diversity-Aware Transferability Spectrum (DATS), a post-training detector targeting input-aware and any-target generative backdoors. DATS reverse-engineers multiple weak candidate triggers per input and constructs a trigger–target transfer matrix whose spectral profile (rank, entropy, and between-candidate exclusivity) distinguishes clean or single-trigger models from input-conditioned or class-conditional generators: clean/single-trigger cases exhibit a low-rank, concentrated spectrum, while input-aware/generative backdoors yield high-rank, high-entropy, and mutually exclusive transfer signatures across candidates. An unsupervised anomaly test on these spectral statistics—optionally combined with ET-style aggregation—flags compromised models without requiring training data or assuming a reusable trigger. This jointly leverages class-pair transferability and multi-target behavior to close a key gap left by detectors that assume a common trigger.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning flexible, tractable meta-distributions over functions for tasks like regression and Bayesian inference, improving on limitations of existing neural process methods. The key insight is to combine denoising diffusion generative modeling with architectural inductive biases for stochastic processes—specifically exchangeability—so the model directly learns to sample finite marginals of function-valued distributions. The proposed method, Neural Diffusion Processes (NDPs), uses a diffusion-based generation scheme together with a custom attention block that enforces permutation invariance and other process properties, training the model to reverse a noising process on function values conditioned on inputs. Empirically, NDPs closely approximate true Bayesian posteriors (e.g., emulating Gaussian processes), outperform neural processes, and support tasks like implicit hyperparameter marginalization, non-Gaussian posterior prediction, and global optimization.

result.text: We propose Baseline-Matched Sampling (BMS) for policy-gradient RL: decouple data collection from the current policy and actively choose a replay-weighted sampling mixture that cancels baseline-induced bias in the expected natural-gradient direction. Concretely, at each iteration we jointly learn a state-value baseline and sampling-mixture weights by enforcing orthogonality of the control-variate term to the policy score under the target policy, implemented via a three-way doubly robust off-policy gradient estimator with truncated importance weights for stability; the sampling mixture is maintained by a replay-aware entropy-regularized objective. This aligns the estimated update with the intended NPG direction even when baselines alter curvature, yielding on softmax policies O(1/t) convergence as in baseline-stabilized NPG and recovering linear rates with entropy regularization, while empirically improving robustness across baseline choices without extra tuning. The design operationalizes prior insights that baselines shape optimization dynamics and that decoupling sampling restores convergence, while leveraging sample-aware entropy and minimax-optimal off-policy gradient estimation to make the decoupling practical and stable.

args.text: CASTLE-PNS: a causal-regularized predictor that jointly learns a sparse input-layer DAG while preferring feature neighborhoods that are both sufficient and necessary for the target. We replace CASTLE’s reconstruction regularizer with a PNS-driven objective computed over stochastic, permutation-resampled mini-environments and steer network gradients toward high-PNS invariant directions, akin to kernel-guided gradient correction without needing environment labels. To stabilize and scale the graph learning, we enforce acyclicity via a log-det penalty within the CASTLE adjacency parameterization. This combination prioritizes stable causal parents over spurious correlates, improving out-of-distribution generalization in heterogeneous sources without explicit environment annotations.

args.text: VectorSDF-Control proposes conditioning diffusion-based text generation/editing on signed distance fields (SDFs) rendered from properly shaped vector fonts (with kerning, ligatures, and script-specific rules) and perspective-warped to the scene, rather than bitmap glyph hints. A differentiable shaping-and-rasterization pipeline supplies crisp, scale-invariant edge priors; training uses web-scale self-supervised in-situ text replacement with an SDF edge-alignment loss (zero-level set) and an OCR-contrastive objective to enforce legibility across multilingual scripts. At inference, alternating optimization jointly refines glyph placement (positions, sizes, warp) and denoising, yielding accurate, style-faithful text on cluttered or oblique backgrounds, and it plugs into existing diffusion backbones without retraining the text encoder.

Manifold-paced GAN training: begin by training on the high-density core of the data manifold and then progressively admit shells of lower-density or undercovered instances as measured in the discriminator/feature space. At each phase, use per-instance augmentation calibrated by density/discrepancy—stronger for high-density examples and semantic-preserving, weaker feature-consistency augmentations for sparse-tail samples—and optionally apply adaptive pseudo-augmentation to seed new shells with the generator’s best current samples. This reconciles pre-training pruning with minority emphasis: early capacity focuses on the core to stabilize, and later phases intentionally expand and upweight tail regions flagged by high discrepancy, improving both fidelity and coverage under limited data. A simple controller that tracks running density and discrepancy schedules shell radius and augmentation strength; we evaluate via FID and precision–recall with subgroup recall gains.

result.text: The paper addresses how to enable large language models (LLMs) to perform reasoning over graph-structured data by encoding graphs as text, identifying why naive conversions fail and which design choices matter. Its key insight is that LLM performance depends critically not just on the downstream task but on the specific textual encoding of the graph and on intrinsic graph structural properties, so that different encoders suit different tasks and graph types. Methodologically, the authors systematically evaluate a palette of graph-to-text encoders across diverse graph reasoning tasks and graph structures, analyze interactions between encoder, task, and graph topology, and demonstrate that choosing appropriate encodings can substantially improve LLM accuracy (by 4.8%–61.8%) on graph reasoning benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of learning solution operators for parametric PDEs with graph-based neural networks while preserving accuracy under mesh refinement, where conventional GNNs truncate long-range interactions and incur discretization-dependent errors. The key insight is to adapt classical multipole ideas to graphs by introducing a multi-level, inducing-point scheme that captures interactions at all scales while keeping computational cost linear in the number of nodes, which makes the learned operator discretization-invariant. Methodologically, the authors build a hierarchical graph neural operator that recursively adds inducing points (equivalently performing multi-resolution matrix factorization of the kernel) to propagate long-range effects across levels, train this multi-graph architecture on PDE solution data, and demonstrate linear-time evaluation and mesh-refinement generalization in experiments.

result.text: We propose Video-to-Stems: a video-conditioned soundtrack generator that jointly models and generates separate musical stems (e.g., drums, bass, melody, ambience) aligned to visual events and long-horizon structure. The method conditions a multi-source joint score model on temporally aligned visual embeddings and rhythm-aware context encoders, while assigning each stem a dedicated cross-attention pathway to instance-tracked visual tokens; training enforces mixture consistency and cross-stem coherence so stems sum to a plausible mix yet remain individually controllable. This enables forward generation, stem-level imputation (e.g., add drums to a silent highlight), and targeted editing by clamping or guiding subsets at inference. We hypothesize this factorized, joint modeling improves rhythmic alignment, semantic correspondence, and editability over single-track V2A baselines, while retaining fast sampling via modern latent/score formulations.

args.text: I-TempoQA proposes joint entity-and-interval answering for temporal KG question answering. It augments a TempoQR-style question encoder with a TEILP-inspired temporal event KG module that conditions differentiable temporal-rule random walks on the question to produce a calibrated time-interval density. The model fuses embedding-based entity plausibility with rule-derived interval likelihoods in a joint decoder that scores (entity, interval) pairs and is trained with a multi-task loss (entity cross-entropy plus interval NLL), yielding path-based explanations. This bridges neural QA and interpretable temporal reasoning, enabling when/during-what-period answers and improving robustness under temporal shifts.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

args.text: We propose Density-Adaptive Smoothed Conservatism (DASC), an offline RL method that learns a state-conditional smoothing radius r(s) from a dataset coverage estimator and enforces conservative value estimates over the r(s)-neighborhood of each dataset state to gain robustness to observation perturbations without excessive pessimism. At evaluation, we certify finite-horizon returns under bounded observation noise by combining global/adaptive smoothing certificates for value-based policies with the learned r(s), yielding larger certified radii where data support is strong and tighter but nontrivial guarantees elsewhere. result.text: The paper addresses the gap in LLM evaluation regarding their ability to quantify uncertainty for unrealizable prediction tasks rather than merely predict correct answers; existing benchmarks focus on accuracy and thus miss whether model probabilities reflect true outcome risk. The key insight is that LLMs can produce useful risk scores but that standard multiple-choice and instruction-tuned setups distort calibration—base models tend to be over-uncertain, instruction tuning drives overconfidence and polarized answer distributions, while chat-style verbalized risk queries improve calibration. To demonstrate this, the authors introduce folktexts, a flexible software toolkit that generates and evaluates LLM-derived risk scores across customizable census-based prediction tasks, compare 17 recent models under diverse prompting schemes (zero-shot multiple-choice vs. verbalized queries), and show systematic miscalibration patterns that conventional realizable benchmarks would not reveal.

args.text: We propose Certifiably Smoothed Guarding (CSG), a prompt-level defense that brings randomized smoothing to discrete prompt space to provide verifiable robustness against jailbreaks. CSG samples an input-dependent distribution over paraphrase and noise operators (e.g., synonym/subphrase substitution, token dropout/insertions, punctuation and formatting variants) applied to a learned guard prefix and the user prompt, aggregates the model’s refusal/comply decision by majority vote, and yields a Monte Carlo certificate that the decision is invariant within a Levenshtein/Hamming radius. We learn the per-input smoothing distribution via bi-level optimization to maximize the smoothed refusal margin while regularizing for benign utility, adapting generalized smoothing theory to discrete operators. Evaluated against token-level and black-box adaptive attacks (including continuous-to-discrete trigger search and tree-based prompt refinement) under standardized settings, CSG targets non-trivial certified regions and empirical robustness with negligible overhead compared to existing guard-prefix methods.

result.text: The paper investigates the alleged incompatibility between label smoothing (LS) and knowledge distillation (KD), motivated by the claim that LS erases the relative information in teacher logits and thus undermines distillation. The key insight is that LS does not uniformly destroy useful inter-class relationships but instead reshapes probability distributions differently for semantically similar versus dissimilar classes, so its harmfulness to KD is conditional rather than absolute. To support this, the authors introduce a metric that quantifies the degree of information erasure in a sample’s representation, and they perform extensive analyses, visualizations, and experiments across image classification, binary networks, and neural machine translation to show the incompatibility view is one-sided and imperfect. They conclude by characterizing circumstances where LS does reduce effectiveness and when it can coexist with or even complement KD.

args.text: We propose Trigger Stability Transferability (TST), a label-free backdoor detector that augments expected transferability with stability tests. After reverse-engineering candidate triggers, TST measures how persistently each trigger enforces a common target across (i) inputs from other classes, (ii) small input/augmentation transformations, and (iii) random low-dimensional subspace perturbations of the model’s penultimate features; it aggregates these into a joint stability–transfer score that clean models rarely exceed. This score separates true backdoors from spurious or brittle patterns, remains effective in binary and multi-attack settings, and can be scanned efficiently over targets via K‑arm selection. TST unifies transferability-based cues with transformation sensitivity to provide domain-agnostic detection without reference data.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning flexible, tractable meta-distributions over functions for tasks like regression and Bayesian inference, improving on limitations of existing neural process methods. The key insight is to combine denoising diffusion generative modeling with architectural inductive biases for stochastic processes—specifically exchangeability—so the model directly learns to sample finite marginals of function-valued distributions. The proposed method, Neural Diffusion Processes (NDPs), uses a diffusion-based generation scheme together with a custom attention block that enforces permutation invariance and other process properties, training the model to reverse a noising process on function values conditioned on inputs. args.text: We propose Rational-Symbol Neural Operators (RaSNO) that model the Fourier multiplier (symbol) of a PDE solution operator as a low-order rational function of frequency and conditioning variables, learned from data. By using Padé-like rational parameterizations, RaSNO can approximate pseudo-differential operators with compact parameter count and reduced depth relative to polynomial/spectral filters, while remaining alias-aware via ReNO-style constraints and bandlimiting losses, and executable on arbitrary point sets with direct spectral evaluation. We further attach a small localized correction layer in physical space to capture non-stationary/boundary effects. We hypothesize this yields discretization-consistent, geometry-agnostic operators with better stability–accuracy tradeoffs on Navier–Stokes, Darcy, and Helmholtz benchmarks, and propose ablations over rational order and aliasing regularization.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of making Bayesian Optimization (BO) robust to distributional shifts in observed contexts by framing BO as a Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem, overcoming limitations of prior work that assumed finite contexts and lacked tractable algorithms. The key insight is that robustness against a broad class of φ-divergences (which includes χ^2, total variation, and KL) admits an equivalent finite-dimensional reformulation, so the infinite-dimensional DRO-BO problem can be solved tractably even with continuous context distributions. The authors develop an algorithm based on this reformulation that is straightforward to implement, prove sublinear regret bounds for the continuous-context setting, and empirically demonstrate superior performance to existing methods, validating both practicality and theoretical guarantees.

result.text: We propose a basis-covariant, SE(3)-equivariant operator predictor for molecular Hamiltonians that learns a continuous kernel H(r, r') via lightweight equivariant message passing and projects it into any atomic-orbital basis, guaranteeing Hermiticity and unitary-basis covariance. The kernel is parameterized as a low-rank sum of separable, symmetry-adapted components with locality-aware sparsification, combining QHNet-style efficient equivariant circuitry with neural-field ideas for wavefunctions to exploit nearsightedness and avoid costly high-rank tensor products. Training uses QH9 Hamiltonians with multiple randomized sub-bases per geometry to enforce basis-agnostic consistency and improve transfer across basis sets and molecular families. The result is a single model that outputs consistent Hamiltonians at different resolutions and supports downstream SCF warm starts and basis-adaptive simulations.

result.text: Develop an amortized Fisher-information streaming active learner that replaces per-batch BAIT optimization with a learned recurrent acquisition policy trained to approximate the Fisher-bound objective under streaming constraints. The policy ingests micro-batch features (uncertainty signals, Jacobian sketches for Fisher surrogates) and a compact coreset state, and outputs which points to query to meet a target rate, while a diversity controller maintains coverage via fast submodular-style updates. We train the policy offline with logged streams using contrastive information bounds as a differentiable surrogate for BAIT’s MLE error bound, and online it adapts to distribution drift via lightweight state updates. args.text: Certified Pessimistic Smoothing for Offline RL: We propose to learn a smoothed, pessimistic Q–policy pair by inserting a randomized smoothing operator into the Bellman backups while training with model-based pessimism on out-of-support rollouts, so the learned policy is both conservative on OOD regions and provably robust to bounded observation perturbations at deployment. Concretely, we adapt policy-smoothing certificates for total return to the offline setting by composing their finite-horizon reward lower bounds with conservative model rollouts, yielding a data-driven certificate that lower-bounds the true return under any adaptive attacker while accounting for model bias. To reduce over-conservatism, we set statewise smoothing radii proportional to offline epistemic uncertainty and restrict pessimism to model-identified OOD regions, producing tighter certificates and stronger nominal performance than pure smoothing or pure pessimism.

args.text: We propose Certified Safety Smoothing for LLMs: a certifiable, prompt-level defense that combines a learned guard prefix with input-dependent randomized smoothing over both continuous embeddings and discrete paraphrases. Concretely, we attach a PAT/RPO-style guard suffix, define a base safety decision as the model’s refusal under a fixed decoding policy, and apply a hybrid noise distribution (Gaussian noise on token embeddings plus synonym/back-translation paraphrases) optimized to maximize the certified safe region; using standard smoothing certificates, we provably guarantee the refusal decision is invariant within a mixed edit-distance/ℓ2 ball around the input. Leveraging recent advances in selecting smoothing distributions and multi-metric certification, we derive tight, per-input certificates via Clopper–Pearson bounds and allow adaptive, input-dependent noise to reduce waterfalls while preserving utility. args.text: Trigger Subspace Probing (TSP): To detect input-aware and X2X generative backdoors that evade single-trigger reverse engineering, we learn for each candidate target a low-dimensional trigger subspace by fitting a small generator or sparse linear basis that maximizes the target logit across many clean held-out inputs from other classes. We then compute an ET-Subspace statistic—the cross-source transfer rate induced by random samples from this subspace—augmented with subspace dimension and target-entropy diagnostics, and flag models showing unusually high transfer concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. A K‑arm style target selection narrows which targets to probe efficiently, and an FCT-style transformation-consistency check validates that the discovered subspace behaves like a trigger rather than a benign feature. This post-training, label-free procedure extends ET/UMD beyond universal triggers and is designed to surface input-aware and class-conditional backdoors.

We propose a query-conditional, steerable mixture-of-expert Neural Process that scales to large context sets via a latent bottleneck while enforcing group equivariance within each expert. Concretely, contexts are compressed into a fixed set of latents as in latent-bottlenecked attentive NPs; a query-dependent gating network attends to these latents to softly route each target to a subset of steerable NP experts whose encoders/decoders are equivariant to the relevant symmetry group. This fuses MoE-NP’s multimodal expressivity with SteerCNP’s symmetry handling while retaining sub-quadratic cost, and an optional Bayesian nonparametric prior over experts enables on-the-fly expert growth under distribution shift. args.text: Current LiDAR–camera 3D detectors either fuse features symmetrically or, like UPIDet, let image auxiliary tasks backprop into the point backbone, but they lack a mechanism to prevent harmful cross‑modal updates when modalities disagree or are unreliable. We propose a reliability‑aware cross‑modal gradient router that predicts a per‑voxel agreement map from reprojection consistency between image‑predicted local geometry (e.g., NLCM/depth cues) and LiDAR occupancy, and uses it to gate and reweight gradients flowing across branches; additionally, gradient surgery orthogonalizes conflicting image‑ and LiDAR‑induced updates. Built atop UPIDet’s point‑to‑pixel link with a BEV fusion head and modality‑maintaining pathways, we add dual auxiliary heads (image NLCM/edges, LiDAR local normals) and pass cross‑modal gradients only through high‑agreement regions while damping them elsewhere. This training‑time router improves far/small‑object detection and robustness under simulated LiDAR dropout or image corruption, with no extra inference cost.

args.text: We propose Rationale-Guided Edge Messaging for text-attributed graphs, addressing the opacity of edge attention in text–structure fusion models and the underuse of LLM rationales beyond node-level features. An LLM is prompted to produce edge-level natural-language explanations conditioned on incident node texts and a small ego-subgraph; these rationales are embedded and injected as multiplicative gates into each layer’s edge message function within a GraphFormers-style interleaved transformer–GNN. Training uses (i) a rationale–attention alignment loss that encourages learned edge attentions to correlate with tokens highlighted in the LLM rationale, and (ii) a counterfactual consistency loss where masking or editing rationale spans leads to predictable changes in edge messages. This yields more accurate, interpretable, and controllable edge, link, and node predictions on TAG benchmarks, outperforming prior textual-edge encoders and text–graph fusion baselines while providing actionable explanations.

result.text: Composed image retrieval (CIR) tackles finding a target image given a reference image plus a relative caption, but prior methods often fuse modalities late or insert a pseudo-word token derived from the reference image, which struggles with complex edits like object removal or attribute changes. The key insight of this paper is that a learned sentence-level prompt appended to the relative caption—rather than a pseudo-word—can capture the necessary transformation information and leverage strong pretrained vision-language models. The authors implement this by using pretrained V-L models (e.g., BLIP-2) to generate and refine a sentence-level prompt concatenated with the relative caption, and train it with image-text contrastive loss plus a text prompt alignment loss so standard text-based image retrieval systems can perform CIR. Empirical results on Fashion-IQ and CIRR show this simple SPRC approach matches or outperforms state-of-the-art CIR methods.

result.text: This paper addresses learning mappings (operators) between infinite-dimensional function spaces, specifically for predicting solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) from input functions, in a way that generalizes across different discretizations and resolutions. The key insight is that a single neural architecture parameterized once can represent such operators by composing nonlinear activations with integral operators whose kernels are implemented via graph-based message-passing, enabling discretization-invariant learning. The method, called a Neural Operator or graph kernel network, approximates the integral kernel by graph convolution/message-passing on a mesh or point cloud, stacks these integral layers with nonlinearities to form an operator network, and trains the shared kernel parameters so the same model generalizes across finite-difference, finite-element, and varying-resolution discretizations. Experiments on PDE tasks demonstrate that this approach achieves the desired resolution and method invariance while matching or improving on state-of-the-art solvers.

To keep computation light and expressive, we compute U_k with a Cartesian-tensor message passing backbone that mixes irreducible components efficiently and augments each layer with MACE-style higher-body messages, capturing many-body interactions in just 1–2 rounds. Compared to direct dense prediction (e.g., QHNet), EF-HNet reduces memory and time from O(N_AO^2) to O(r N_AO) while preserving angular-channel structure, and we regularize r adaptively with sparsity penalties tied to distance and angular momentum selection rules. We train with spectral-consistency losses (eigenvalues and density-matrix constraints) in addition to elementwise supervision; on QH9 we expect a better accuracy–speed Pareto and improved transfer across molecules and basis sets.

The key insight is that distillation can improve aggregate accuracy while degrading performance on specific classes that exceed the student’s capacity to reproduce, and that the prevalence of such classes correlates with the capacity gap between teacher and student. The authors propose a simple Teach Less, Learn More (TLLM) framework that detects and discards these undistillable classes during student training, effectively preventing the student from being misled by teacher outputs it cannot emulate. Empirical results across datasets and architectures show that TLLM consistently improves student performance over standard and state-of-the-art distillation methods.

args.text: We propose Certificate-Guided Memory Routing for long-video LMMs: a query-conditioned mechanism that estimates a temporal “certificate” over video segments and allocates KV-cache and retrieval budgets accordingly to support hour-scale referring reasoning. At inference, a head-wise adaptive eviction controller assigns per-head, per-segment budgets from the KV cache guided by certificate scores, while a landmark-token index enables random-access retrieval to high-scoring temporal blocks within a blockwise long-context attention scheme. To reduce token load, low-scoring spans are compressed into object-centric textualizations, and training uses a curriculum with synthetic multi-hop “needle chains” embedded in long videos to calibrate retrieval and temporal grounding. This unifies controlled evaluation with efficient memory and routing, aiming to deliver strong long-horizon performance with substantially smaller active context.

result.text: We propose Subspace-Shattering Unlearnable Examples (SSUE), a defense that meta-optimizes per-example perturbations so the informative signal is dispersed into different low-dimensional subspaces across data augmentations and training checkpoints, breaking the fixed-subspace assumption exploited by simple linear purification (e.g., orthogonal projection). Concretely, SSUE keys an augmentation-aware perturbation schedule to each sample ID, uses a self-ensemble-over-checkpoints objective to enforce cross-time inconsistency of useful features, and couples classwise geometry regularization so poisoned representations remain class-consistent yet misaligned across views. To maximize transfer, the loss jointly poisons multiple pretext objectives (contrastive, BYOL/SimSiam-style predictive, and masked reconstruction) so that both supervised and self-supervised pipelines inherit the shattered subspaces. We hypothesize SSUE will outperform CSD- and SEM-style noise and SEP under adversarial training and approximate unlearning, while resisting linear and reconstruction-based purification by design, and validate on CIFAR/ImageNet and CL benchmarks with stress tests against known purification and unlearning procedures.

result.text: Gradient-Guided Consistency Augmentation (GGCA): a per-layer controller for GAN discriminators that continuously estimates the real–fake gradient-norm gap and uses it to (i) adapt augmentation strength/probabilities and (ii) localize consistency losses to feature layers where the gap is largest. In contrast to global ADA/DiffAugment and naive consistency schemes, GGCA selects only margin-preserving transforms and targets to explicitly reduce the measured gap, avoiding artifact-inducing alignment while preserving generator fidelity. To stabilize these localized targets under strong transforms, we add a lightweight feature-quantization head and an instance-contrastive objective that align augmented codes of the same sample yet keep real/fake codes separable, yielding robust, low-variance signals. This unifies adaptive augmentation, gradient-gap regularization, and contrastive/instance-discrimination in a single controller, and we expect significant FID/diversity gains in 1–10k image regimes on CIFAR/FFHQ/LSUN.
