args.text: I propose Role-Centric Counterfactual Value Decomposition (RCVD): learn compact, identifiable role embeddings with a contrastive mutual-information objective and attention-conditioned policies, then decompose Q-values at the role level rather than per agent. A duplex-dueling QPLEX-style mixer aggregates per-role advantages to satisfy IGM in a low-rank role space, and credits are projected to agents via soft role assignments while a contrastive identity-aware term encourages discriminable temporal credits. To sharpen credit and reduce variance without bias, we add action-oblivious future-conditioned baselines built on role-relevant team events as counterfactual critics during CTDE. We hypothesize this role-first factorization yields more stable specialization, faster learning, and transferable coordination in SMAC/GRF with dynamic team sizes compared to ROMA/ACORM, CIA-augmented VD, and QPLEX backbones.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of producing useful synthetic data under differential privacy constraints, where existing private generative models struggle to capture high-dimensional data distributions and yield low utility samples. The key insight is that, instead of privately learning the full data distribution, it is easier and more effective to privately optimize a small set of representative samples guided by discriminative signals from downstream tasks. The authors propose a method that directly generates and refines a private “private set” of exemplars by leveraging task-specific discriminative information during training, which reduces the complexity of private learning and concentrates privacy budget on the most task-relevant points. Empirically, this simple approach substantially improves downstream utility compared to prior state-of-the-art differentially private generative methods.

We propose an anytime, budget-aware inverse design framework that tightly interleaves neural-operator learning with neural-adjoint optimization, choosing at each step whether to optimize through the surrogate or to spend compute refining it. Concretely, an ensemble neural operator (e.g., FNO or hybrid GNN+coarse solver) provides gradients and an uncertainty estimate; a controller schedules either (i) a surrogate-based gradient step when predicted improvement per unit time is high and uncertainty low, or (ii) an active high-fidelity PDE query at designs selected to maximally reduce local surrogate error, followed by rapid incremental operator updates. The loop includes lightweight physics-residual checks and gradient-disagreement tests to trigger active refinement, yielding calibrated gradients over long horizons and improved time-to-solution versus pure two-phase or purely sampling-based methods. We evaluate on PDE-constrained control and fluid-structure inverse design, showing faster convergence under fixed wall-clock budgets and better final designs by focusing surrogate capacity on the optimizer’s visited manifold.

args.text: We propose Certifiably Robust Offline RL via Uncertainty-Adaptive Smoothing, which learns a value-based policy with conservative Bellman updates over local perturbation neighborhoods and provides certified lower bounds on cumulative return under adaptive observation attacks. Concretely, we train an ensemble Q to quantify epistemic uncertainty and set a state-dependent smoothing radius; we then enforce conservative value regularization on perturbed neighbors of dataset states and learn a smoothed Q/policy to enable randomized-smoothing-style certificates. At deployment, we inject Gaussian noise into observations to obtain finite-horizon, adaptive-attack return certificates while the conservatism calibrated by uncertainty preserves safety under distribution shift. This unifies pessimistic offline training with certifiable robustness, yielding bounds that tighten where data coverage is strong and uncertainty is low, and degrade gracefully otherwise.

We propose an alignment-aware selective state-space layer that preserves near-linear scaling while enabling robust long-range comparison and recall. The layer computes a lightweight, differentiable drop-alignment between token sequences (a banded variant of Drop-DTW) to identify inlier correspondences and uses the resulting path to modulate a quasiseparable mixer instantiated via the Transformer–SSM duality, effectively attending along the alignment path without full attention. Concretely, we condition liquid SSM transition parameters on alignment gates so the selective dynamics amplify recalled tokens and pairwise comparisons while suppressing outliers, and we train with a consistency loss to teacher attention maps plus a self-supervised alignment objective. This design marries H3’s recall/comparison strengths with Hydra-style quasiseparable mixing and Mamba-2 dual formulations, yielding an architecture expected to outperform attention on noisy, very long contexts at near-linear compute.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently and precisely evaluating video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), where existing benchmarks are costly to build and often conflate multiple skills. The method, VideoNIAH, automates creation of video-query-response pairs by programmatically planting needles and applying predefined query templates to produce VNBench, a suite of retrieval, ordering, and counting tasks designed to probe temporal perception, chronological ordering, and spatio-temporal coherence across varied video lengths. result.text: The paper addresses Novel Class Discovery (NCD), i.e., how to leverage a labeled set of known classes to discover novel classes in an unlabeled set, by providing theoretical foundations for when and how known classes help. Its key insight is that NCD can be cast as learning a graph-theoretic representation whose adjacency structure encodes class relationships across known and unknown domains, and that minimizing a carefully designed spectral contrastive loss is equivalent to factorizing this adjacency matrix—yielding provable error bounds and a necessary-and-sufficient condition for successful discovery. Methodologically, the authors propose the NCD Spectral Contrastive Loss (NSCL) which trains embeddings by enforcing spectral factorization of the learned graph, derive theoretical guarantees linking loss minimization to recovery of novel classes, and validate empirically that NSCL matches or outperforms strong baselines on benchmarks.

args.text: Temporal Trigger Consistency (TTC) for backdoor detection in video trackers: we extend label-free expected transferability and feature-consistency tests to the temporal domain to expose few-frame backdoors in VOT. We reverse-engineer a minimal perturbation on a short subsequence that induces a specific failure mode (e.g., drift-to-background), then measure its cross-video temporal transfer by applying it to diverse objects and computing two scores: (i) Temporal Expected Transferability (T-ET), the consistency of induced failure direction and failure-time distribution across videos, and (ii) Temporal Feature Consistency Gap (T-FCT), the sensitivity of internal feature trajectories to temporal augmentations (frame-rate jitter, motion blur) relative to clean behavior. Clean trackers show low T-ET and small T-FCT gaps, while backdoored trackers exhibit high temporal transfer and instability; these signals also seed a lightweight unlearning pass that alternates adversarial temporal augmentation with attention-alignment fine-tuning to scrub the trigger.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressiveness of Neural Processes (NPs), whose reliance on a single global latent variable hinders modeling complex, multimodal data-generating processes and restricts their applicability in meta-learning and few-shot settings. Its key insight is that augmenting NPs with a mixture-of-experts mechanism yields a richer, more flexible meta-representation by allowing multiple specialized latent components to capture diverse modes and local structure across tasks while preserving exchangeability. The method, Mixture of Expert Neural Processes (MoE-NPs), integrates a gating network and multiple expert NPs so that for each context the model infers a mixture over expert latents and aggregates expert predictions to produce task-conditional outputs; this architecture is trained end-to-end and applied to few-shot supervised and meta-reinforcement learning benchmarks, where it shows improved generalization to unseen tasks.

result.text: The paper investigates how commonly used baselines in policy gradient methods affect optimization beyond merely reducing gradient variance, showing that baseline choice can change the optimization dynamics and even harm learning despite lower variance. The key insight is that baselines influence the update direction and curvature of the expected update—so two baselines with identical variance can lead to different trajectories and convergence properties, and some baselines can cause natural policy gradient to converge to suboptimal policies for any stepsize when sampling is tied to the current policy. The authors analyze simple illustrative examples and theoretical conditions, and propose decoupling the sampling policy from the current policy to restore robust convergence for a much broader set of baselines, arguing for treating stochasticity in updates more carefully than by variance reduction alone.

result.text: The paper tackles how to enable frozen large language models (LLMs) to both understand and generate non-linguistic modalities (e.g., images, videos) without changing the LLM weights. The key insight is to map pixels to and from the LLM’s own lexical space via a hierarchical "semantic pyramid" of tokens that jointly encode high-level semantics and fine-grained visual detail, so the LLM can reason about and produce visual content using its native vocabulary. Methodologically, SPAE trains an encoder–decoder that converts images into sequences of interpretable lexical tokens aligned with the LLM’s vocabulary and reconstructs images from those tokens using multiscale latent representations, then uses in-context prompting with frozen PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5 to perform and evaluate multimodal understanding and generation tasks. This approach yields the first demonstration of frozen LLM image generation and substantially improves image understanding performance (over 25% relative) under the same frozen-LM setting.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of large accuracy drop in ANN-to-SNN conversion when SNNs run with very few time-steps, which limits their practical deployment on neuromorphic hardware. The key insight is that conversion error is dominated by "offset spikes"—cases where a neuron fires one more or one fewer spike than its target rate—and that correcting this discrete spiking offset can greatly reduce error at low latency. The authors propose calibrating the initial membrane potential by computing and applying an optimal shift that counteracts the offset spike bias (and show this shift can be applied iteratively for further gains), and they provide theoretical justification for the optimal shift and empirical results demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet with as few as six time-steps.

The proposed GraphFormers architecture interleaves transformer layers with GNN layers and is trained with a progressive strategy that first uses manipulated data and then original data to strengthen graph integration; evaluations on three large benchmarks show it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with similar efficiency.

result.text: The paper addresses temporal knowledge graph event forecasting, specifically the difficulty of predicting future interactions for entities lacking useful historical recurrence or periodicity. result.text: We propose Conformal Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (CESS), a black-box, distribution-free procedure that turns self-consistency sampling into a risk-controlled stopping rule with finite-sample guarantees. On a calibration set, we run deep self-consistency to learn a mapping from the trajectory of vote-share (and simple diversity features) to correctness, then derive nondecreasing stopping boundaries via conformal calibration so that when the live vote-trajectory crosses the boundary we stop and output the modal answer with 1−α coverage; if the boundary is not reached within a budget, we abstain. result.text: We propose Trigger Stability Transferability (TST), a label-free backdoor detector that augments expected transferability with stability tests. After reverse-engineering candidate triggers, TST measures how persistently each trigger enforces a common target across (i) inputs from other classes, (ii) small input/augmentation transformations, and (iii) random low-dimensional subspace perturbations of the model’s penultimate features; it aggregates these into a joint stability–transfer score that clean models rarely exceed. This score separates true backdoors from spurious or brittle patterns, remains effective in binary and multi-attack settings, and can be scanned efficiently over targets via K‑arm selection. TST unifies transferability-based cues with transformation sensitivity to provide domain-agnostic detection without reference data.

result.text: EffiLearner tackles the problem of inefficient runtime and memory characteristics in code generated by large language models (LLMs) by introducing a self-optimization loop that closes the gap between functional correctness and performance. The key insight is that concrete execution profiles—measured execution time and memory usage—provide actionable, model-readable signals that an LLM can use to iteratively refine its output toward more efficient implementations. Concretely, EffiLearner generates code with an LLM, executes the code locally to collect execution time and total memory usage profiles, feeds those profiles back as feedback prompts to the same LLM, and repeats this generate-execute-refine cycle until improvements plateau; extensive evaluations on EffiBench, HumanEval, and MBPP across multiple open- and closed-source models show large reductions in execution time and memory (e.g., 87.1% ET and 90.8% TMU reduction for StarCoder2-15B).

Methodologically, the authors introduce LORIS, which uses a latent diffusion probabilistic model to synthesize waveforms and a set of temporal conditioning encoders that encode rhythmic visual context for long-term generation, and they validate the approach across extended scenarios (dance and sports) on a new benchmark with improved metrics and baselines, showing state-of-the-art musical quality and rhythmic correspondence.

result.text: I propose score–adjoint posterior sampling for PDE-constrained inverse design: learn a diffusion prior over feasible parameter fields or a latent code, pair it with a neural-operator surrogate of the forward PDE, and run preconditioned Langevin dynamics whose drift combines the prior score with adjoint gradients of the surrogate likelihood. Use the surrogate’s Gauss–Newton metric as a Riemannian preconditioner and an active error-control loop that occasionally triggers high-fidelity PDE solves where surrogate gradient uncertainty or disagreement is high, refining the operator online. This unifies generative, sampling-based recovery with neural-adjoint search, improving time-to-solution by rapidly exploring high-probability regions while maintaining physics consistency and yielding calibrated uncertainty over designs. We will benchmark under time-to-solution across fluid/FSI and metamaterial tasks, comparing to pure diffusion-PDE samplers and pure neural-adjoint optimizers.

The paper addresses active learning for deep neural networks in realistic streaming scenarios where data arrive sequentially and labels must be requested on the fly rather than from an offline pool. Its key insight is that effective streaming active learning can be achieved by balancing per-sample uncertainty with diversity among a small group of recently seen points, thereby matching a target query rate without hand-tuned hyperparameters. The proposed method, VeSSAL, examines incoming data in small batches, scores candidates by a combined uncertainty-diversity objective, selects a subset to query immediately to satisfy the query budget, and updates the model incrementally; this streaming sampling scheme enables practical batch active learning for DNNs on large, fragmented, or human-in-the-loop datasets.

result.text: FetchSGD addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of heavy communication costs and degraded convergence when client participation is sparse. The key insight is to use a linear, mergeable Count Sketch to compress client model updates so that momentum and error accumulation can be maintained centrally inside the sketch rather than on each client, which preserves state across intermittent clients and enables high compression without losing critical optimization history. Concretely, each client sketches its local gradient/update with a Count Sketch, the server merges these sketches to form an aggregate sketch, performs momentum and error correction in sketch space, and reconstructs sparse updates for model updates; the authors prove convergence guarantees for this procedure and validate it empirically on ResNets and a transformer showing strong communication savings and robust convergence.

result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. The authors propose three consistency-based measures computed from random generations, evaluate them across eleven models (open and closed) and nine reasoning datasets, and show these measures reduce calibration error compared to prior approaches; they also find that factors like intermediate explanations, model scale, and larger sample sizes improve calibration while instruction-tuning hinders it, and that consistency-derived confidence can even boost downstream performance, with practical guidance on picking metrics based on model traits such as instruction-tuning and RLHF exposure.

args.text: We propose Prompt Randomized Smoothing for Certified Refusal (PRoSCR): combine an adversarially learned guard prefix with an input-dependent discrete smoothing distribution over paraphrase wrappers, synonym substitutions, and template variants sampled at inference, then aggregate with majority/refusal voting. By tailoring the smoothing distribution to edit-distance (or embedding-based) threat models and invoking non-Gaussian/randomized smoothing theory, we can compute Monte Carlo certificates that lower-bound refusal probability under any perturbation within a bounded prompt neighborhood. We jointly train the guard prefix and the smoothing distribution to maximize the certified refusal radius subject to utility constraints on benign prompts. This yields certifiable robustness to jailbreak-style prompt perturbations while preserving the lightweight, deployable nature of prompt-level defenses.

result.text: We propose Anchor-Needle Provenance (ANP), a training-and-evaluation framework for long-form video LMMs that enforces answer-with-evidence behavior on hour-scale inputs. We plant semantically plausible, multimodal "anchors" (synthetic yet decoupled events) across long videos and pair them with question templates; during training, the model must both answer and return explicit pointers to the referenced segments via learned landmark tokens over temporal blocks, while using hierarchical temporal-window attention to scale. This couples contrastive segment–text alignment with landmark-mediated random access to teach precise referring reasoning and reduce overreliance on world knowledge. We adapt needle-in-a-haystack recipes to the long-video regime and extend referring-reasoning benchmarks with provenance-based scoring (answer correctness plus cited segments), expecting substantial gains in long-video QA and retrieval.

args.text: Behavior-Fisher Projected Mirror PPO (BF-PMPPO) measures trust-region steps with a replay-weighted Fisher metric computed per state from the behavior distribution, so mirror-descent updates shrink in poorly covered directions and expand along well-covered ones. Concretely, we take an off-policy PPO-style gradient step and then apply a differentiable projection layer that performs a closed-form ellipsoidal projection of Gaussian policy parameters under the behavior-Fisher geometry, followed by an explicit behavior-support filter/projection to prevent OOD actions. The trust-region radius adapts online using an off-policyness score, yielding MDPO/CPI-like improvement guarantees while enabling safe, effective sample reuse without conservative density matching. We expect improved stability and sample efficiency over Off-Policy PPO and STR on continuous control, especially in heterogeneous datasets with strongly anisotropic coverage.

args.text: Counterfactual Cross-Modal Causal Probes (C3P) frames multimodal fake-news detection as learning an event-centric structural causal model over text, image/video frames, audio transcripts, comments, and publisher nodes, so that veracity depends on modality-invariant mechanisms rather than spurious correlations. A learned intervention policy selects minimal cross-modal edits—e.g., swapping comments among semantically similar posts, substituting visually equivalent frames, or masking modality-specific cues—and the detection score is the stability gap of the prediction under these counterfactuals; truthful items remain invariant, while fabrications that hinge on cross-modal inconsistencies flip, yielding compact, human-interpretable rationales. We initialize causal edges with cognition-aware fusion and coherence constraints and ground entities with compact knowledge subgraphs to avoid noisy external evidence. We benchmark on short-video settings with rich social context, targeting OOD robustness and pattern-level explanations beyond prior fusion or knowledge-injection methods.

We propose Active Token Foveation for multimodal LLMs: an autoregressive model that decides on-the-fly how many and which visual tokens to retrieve, starting from a tiny coarse representation and iteratively requesting fine tokens only for text-conditioned uncertain regions under a global compute budget. A learnable controller monitors decoding state and cross-modal attentions to (a) pull region- and layer-specific finer tokens from a nested encoder, (b) inject them late via stacked layer-wise token entry, and (c) merge redundancies with cross-guided soft matching, yielding a compact yet informative context. Training uses a budget-aware objective that imitates oracle instancewise allocations and/or RL with a reward trading accuracy against token cost, leveraging semantic-equivariant tokenization to maintain coherence across refinement levels. This token-on-demand loop closes the gap between fixed-length and oracle allocations, improving small-budget accuracy and enabling foveated high-resolution and streaming reasoning.

result.text: The paper addresses controlled paraphrase generation, aiming to preserve original meaning while varying lexical novelty in outputs. The key insight is that combining retrieval-augmented context with parameter-efficient prompt tuning can both adapt large pretrained language models for paraphrasing and enable explicit control over novelty via specialized prompt tokens. The method introduces Retrieval Augmented Prompt Tuning (RAPT), which conditions prompt-tuned models on retrieved paraphrase examples, and Novelty Conditioned RAPT (NC-RAPT), which appends learned novelty-control tokens to prompts to steer generation toward different lexical distances from the input. Experiments on four datasets show these approaches maintain semantic fidelity while effectively inducing adjustable levels of lexical novelty.

A differentiable sampler outputs per-point selection logits (e.g., Gumbel top-k) and is trained so the LiDAR-only student’s intermediate BEV features and final boxes align with a fusion teacher (e.g., BEVFusion/UVTR), encouraging selection of points most informative for the teacher’s decisions on small/distant objects. result.text: The paper tackles the problem that existing iterative preference-optimization methods improve general instruction following but fail to substantially boost multi-step reasoning performance; the authors aim to better select and refine Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces that lead to correct answers. Their key insight is to directly optimize preferences over competing CoT candidates by emphasizing the winning versus losing reasoning steps that causally lead to the correct answer, and that combining a DPO-style preference loss with an additional negative log-likelihood term is crucial to steer the model toward correct reasoning trajectories. Methodologically, they iteratively generate multiple CoT samples, label winners and losers according to answer correctness, and train the model with a modified DPO objective plus an NLL term to increase probability of winning steps and decrease that of losing steps; repeated iterations yield steady reasoning improvements. Empirically, this procedure—applied to Llama-2-70B-Chat using only in-dataset examples—substantially raises accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, and ARC-Challenge (e.g., GSM8K from 55.6% to 81.6%, and 88.7% with 32-sample majority voting).

args.text: Mask-and-Stitch Merging proposes a three-stage, tuning-light pipeline for multi-task weight fusion. First, we predict a fast permutation alignment between task-specific checkpoints with a symmetry-equivariant aligner, then apply TALL-style consensus masking to preserve task-support weights while safely averaging the remainder with uncertainty-weighting. Second, we attach tiny per-task stitching adapters and train them on a small, unlabeled calibration set to match the original models’ intermediate representations, removing the merged model’s representation bias. This hybrid of alignment, sparse preservation, and unsupervised stitching aims to recover near single-task accuracy without per-task checkpoints, and should be especially effective when tasks partly overlap but exhibit strong layer-local conflicts.

Constraining the coupling to be low-rank yields a cheap alternating-update estimator that preserves marginals yet captures global transport structure, providing variance-reduced training targets and inducing straighter, near-OT trajectories that integrate in few steps. The convex-potential parameterization further aligns the learned flow with quadratic-cost OT, combining variance reduction and monotonicity to approach one-step generation while remaining simulation-free. We hypothesize that with rank as a knob, NFEs and transport cost drop sharply versus standard multisample FM, recovering OFM-like behavior at modest ranks and scaling to high-dimensional images.

result.text: The paper addresses how to make large language models (LLMs), especially closed‑source black‑box APIs, reliably express uncertainty to support trustworthy decisions; prior approaches needing internal access or fine‑tuning are often infeasible for these models. Its key insight is that black‑box elicitation can be decomposed into three controllable components—verbal confidence prompts, sampling multiple responses, and aggregating consistency—and that human‑inspired prompting plus consistency‑based aggregation can substantially reduce but not eliminate LLM overconfidence, with larger models exhibiting better calibration and failure prediction. The authors implement and benchmark a systematic suite of prompting strategies, sampling schemes, and aggregation methods across five LLMs (including GPT‑4, LLaMA 2 Chat) and diverse datasets, evaluating calibration and failure prediction against white‑box baselines; they show black‑box methods narrow the performance gap (e.g., AUROC improvements toward white‑box 0.605 from 0.522) but still struggle on hard, domain‑expert tasks, highlighting room for future work.

args.text: We propose Token-Edit Randomized Smoothing for Safety (TERSS): a certifiable wrapper that predicts refusal via a smoothed safety head over randomized token-edit noise (insert/replace/delete, including control/system tokens), yielding a provable radius in Hamming/edit space within which no jailbreak can flip the decision. We train the base refusal scorer and/or a guard prefix with adversarial tuning against strong attacker families (logprob-guided restricted-token search, ADC-style continuous-to-discrete suffixes, TAP-style tree search, and I-FSJ system-token injections) while maximizing the smoothed margin, leveraging recent non-Gaussian and general smoothing theory to choose discrete noise tailored to these threat models. At inference, Monte Carlo certificates provide per-prompt guarantees (e.g., robustness to any suffix up to k tokens from a chosen vocabulary), and the same threat-model parameters integrate cleanly into standardized evaluations to avoid incomplete-adaptivity pitfalls. This marries empirical prompt defenses with certifiable robustness, turning safety checks from best-effort into verifiable guarantees under realistic jailbreak budgets.

result.text: The paper addresses formal verification of closed-loop dynamical systems controlled by neural networks by computing precise reachable sets, a task made difficult because existing set representations—Taylor models for dynamical systems and zonotopes for neural networks—lose dependency information when converted back and forth, causing error blowup over control cycles. args.text: We propose Anchored Spectral Prototype Discovery (ASPD) for universal category discovery under domain shift and ambiguous taxonomies. ASPD learns a semantic representation decomposed into a prototype-anchored subspace that follows the labeled taxonomy and an orthogonal discovery subspace for novel classes by (i) anchoring eigenvectors of a target affinity graph to matched source-class prototypes via bipartite matching, (ii) co-factorizing the graph with these anchors while using mutual-information–based self-labeling on the target to stabilize cluster assignments, and (iii) minimizing mutual information between semantic and domain features to disentangle shift. A granularity prior based on minimum-length categorical codes adaptively splits or merges clusters in the discovery subspace, enabling hierarchical unknown discovery while preserving known-class alignment. This unified objective targets stronger generalized category discovery and universal domain adaptation under multi-domain shift.

We propose Equivariant Latent-Bottleneck Neural Diffusion Processes (ELB-NDP), which combine diffusion-based meta-distributions over functions with group-equivariant, fixed-size latent summaries of the context to achieve symmetry-respecting predictions and sub-quadratic scaling. A steerable/equivariant set encoder maps context pairs into a small set of latents, and an equivariant score network drives conditional reverse diffusion for target function values by cross-attending to these latents, ensuring both exchangeability and equivariance by construction. This marries the accurate posterior sampling of neural diffusion processes with ConvNP/SteerCNP symmetry priors and the latent bottleneck efficiency of attentive NPs, enabling coherent samples for large, structured fields under rotations and translations. We evaluate on equivariant GP emulation, weather/vector-field forecasting, and high-resolution image inpainting with group transformations.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficient learning of directed acyclic graph (DAG) structures from data, where existing continuous optimization approaches enforce acyclicity via costly iterative constraints. The key insight is that weighted adjacency matrices of DAGs exactly correspond to gradients of graph potential functions, so one can search for DAGs by projecting arbitrary weighted graphs onto the space of gradient fields (i.e., curl-free graphs) instead of imposing acyclicity directly. The proposed method, DAG-NoCurl, therefore computes an initial (possibly cyclic) solution to the unconstrained optimization and then applies a Hodge decomposition to extract and retain only the gradient component, yielding an acyclic weighted adjacency matrix; this two-step projection-based algorithm achieves similar accuracy but substantially faster runtimes than prior constrained methods on linear and generalized structural equation benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the need for reliable semantic similarity metrics to evaluate reformulation tasks like style transfer, paraphrase, and MT, noting that current metrics are widely used despite unclear fidelity to human judgment. Methodologically, the authors compile a new dataset of 14,000 sentence pairs annotated for semantic similarity and use it to compare over a dozen automatic metrics, reporting correlations with human labels and demonstrating WMD’s superior, though still imperfect, reliability for measuring semantic equivalence in paraphrase/style-transfer scenarios.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of training deep spiking neural networks (SNNs) with backpropagation: existing methods struggle with the discontinuous, event-driven nature of spikes and require many time steps (high latency) to reach competitive performance. The key insight is to decompose error backpropagation into two complementary dependency types—inter-neuron dependencies via presynaptic firing times (capturing the all-or-none spike events) and intra-neuron dependencies via the continuous temporal evolution of each neuron’s internal state—so gradients more accurately reflect temporal spike causality. The proposed Temporal Spike Sequence Learning Backpropagation (TSSL-BP) explicitly models and backpropagates through both dependency classes, enabling precise temporal credit assignment and efficient training of deep SNNs in only a few time steps. Empirically, TSSL-BP shortens required temporal windows and improves accuracy on image classification benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10), making spike-based deep learning more scalable and practical.

result.text: The paper addresses how to automatically discover useful roles to decompose complex multi-agent tasks so learning scales with many agents. The key insight is that parameterizing the integral kernel of a neural operator in Fourier space yields an expressive, globally-aware, and computationally efficient representation that naturally handles convolutional-like interactions across the domain. result.text: The paper addresses detecting backdoor (Trojan) attacks in classifiers for the general X2X setting where multiple arbitrary source classes may each map to arbitrary target classes—a setting unsolved by prior (mostly single-target) detectors. result.text: The paper tackles poor generalization and inefficient training of deep spiking neural networks (SNNs) caused by non-differentiable spike activations and the inadequacy of surrogate gradient (SG) methods, which lose momentum and lead to sharp minima and temporal brittleness. result.text: The paper addresses the practical challenge of imputing missing values in tabular data, balancing the simplicity and flexibility of iterative conditional modeling against the scalability and capacity of deep generative methods. result.text: We propose Active Token Foveation for multimodal LLMs: an autoregressive model that decides on-the-fly how many and which visual tokens to retrieve, starting from a tiny coarse representation and iteratively requesting fine tokens only for text-conditioned uncertain regions under a global compute budget. Its key insight is to mimic diverse human "reading habits" to guide deeper, cognition-aware fusion of multimodal features and to explicitly reason about semantic coherence and deviation between modalities (including user comments) to expose inconsistencies indicative of falsehood. The proposed Multi-Reading Habits Fusion Reasoning (MRHFR) network implements a cognition-aware fusion layer that learns dependencies among visual, textual, and other modal representations according to three distilled reading habits, and a coherence-constraint reasoning layer that measures semantic consistency between comments and each modality and constrains unimodal-induced deviations from the multimodal content. Experiments on two public datasets show MRHFR improves detection performance and offers a new paradigm for capturing multimodal inconsistencies.

result.text: The paper addresses Bayesian structure learning for Bayesian networks, aiming to infer graph structure from data while capturing posterior uncertainty over both edges and conditional distribution parameters to support tasks like active causal discovery and interventions. The key insight is to represent discrete graph structures via a continuous latent probabilistic graph embedding, enabling fully differentiable inference that is agnostic to the form of local conditionals and thus compatible with complex, e.g., neural-network-based, conditional models. The method, DiBS, uses this continuous latent representation within a variational inference framework to jointly approximate the posterior over graph structures and parameters, leveraging gradient-based optimization to efficiently learn distributions over structural models. Empirically, DiBS yields more accurate joint posterior inference on simulated and real datasets compared to prior joint-inference approaches.

result.text: We propose Active Token Foveation for multimodal LLMs: an autoregressive model that decides on-the-fly how many and which visual tokens to retrieve, starting from a tiny coarse representation and iteratively requesting fine tokens only for text-conditioned uncertain regions under a global compute budget. A learnable controller monitors decoding state and cross-modal attentions to (a) pull region- and layer-specific finer tokens from a nested encoder, (b) inject them late via stacked layer-wise token entry, and (c) merge redundancies with cross-guided soft matching, yielding a compact yet informative context. Training uses a budget-aware objective that imitates oracle instancewise allocations and/or RL with a reward trading accuracy against token cost, leveraging semantic-equivariant tokenization to maintain coherence across refinement levels. This token-on-demand loop closes the gap between fixed-length and oracle allocations, improving small-budget accuracy and enabling foveated high-resolution and streaming reasoning.

result.text: The paper tackles the trade-off between energy-efficient spiking neural networks (SNNs) that require many time-steps when produced by ANN-to-SNN conversion and the high cost of training SNNs from scratch with spike-based backpropagation. args.text: We propose Distributionally Robust Prior-augmented Joint Entropy Search (DR-JES), which integrates domain priors into information-theoretic BO while hedging against misspecification. Starting from a user-specified prior over the optimizer (and optionally its value or other function properties), we define a φ-divergence ambiguity set around this prior and choose evaluations that maximize the worst-case expected reduction in the joint entropy of the optimal input–output pair, implemented by reweighting JES’s Monte Carlo estimator via standard DRO duals. This unifies piBO/ColaBO-style prior biasing with joint-entropy lookahead and ensures graceful degradation whose sensitivity scales with the ambiguity radius, reducing to JES or prior-weighted JES as the radius tends to ∞ or 0. Practically, DR-JES reuses GP fantasies with a small inner convex problem per acquisition step and can adaptively tune the ambiguity radius using posterior predictive checks to anneal toward informative priors when data agree.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that point masked autoencoders for self-supervised point cloud learning can rely on provided patch centers rather than encoder representations, which prevents encoders from learning strong semantic features. They implement this by adding a Predicting Center Module (PCM) that shares encoder parameters and uses cross-attention to predict masked-patch centers, which are then used by the decoder instead of the true centers; this simple change yields more efficient pretraining and substantial classification gains over prior Point-MAE baselines.

result.text: LongVideoBench addresses the lack of public benchmarks for evaluating large multimodal models (LMMs) on long, interleaved video-language inputs by introducing a question-answering dataset that tests long-term multimodal understanding up to hour-long videos. result.text: The paper addresses learning neural networks that must satisfy domain-specific monotonicity constraints—i.e., outputs should not decrease when certain input features increase—while still using expressive ReLU models. The key insight is to combine counterexample-guided correction at prediction time with counterexample-driven training: searching for inputs that violate monotonicity, projecting or repairing predictions to satisfy the constraints, and then using those counterexamples as additional training data to bias the model toward monotonic behavior. The method requires no restriction of the ReLU hypothesis class: a verifier/search procedure finds monotonicity violations, a repair step enforces monotonicity on predictions (provably at inference), and an iterative loop injects discovered counterexamples into learning so the network gradually internalizes the constraint; implemented in the COMET tool, this approach yields state-of-the-art monotonic learners on real datasets and can improve unconstrained models by leveraging monotonicity as an inductive bias.

The paper tackles open-vocabulary object detection, i.e., detecting objects described by arbitrary text despite scarce labeled detection data for many categories. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning from eigenvector-based spectral representations on graphs and meshes while correctly handling the intrinsic symmetries of eigenvectors—namely sign flips and arbitrary orthonormal basis choices within degenerate eigenspaces—which otherwise break downstream learning and limit expressiveness. The key insight is to build architectures that are provably invariant to these symmetries, so any function learned from eigenvectors respects sign- and basis-equivalence and thus depends only on the intrinsic spectral information. The authors propose two neural architectures, SignNet for sign-flip invariance and BasisNet for full basis invariance, prove universal approximation results showing these networks can represent any continuous invariant function of eigenvectors, and show that when applied to Laplacian eigenvectors they strictly generalize existing spectral graph convolutions, positional encodings, and other spectral invariants. Empirically, SignNet and BasisNet outperform prior spectral baselines on tasks including molecular graph regression, expressive graph representation learning, and neural fields on triangle meshes.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of predicting multimodal, socially-aware future trajectories (intent) of multiple pedestrians for safe autonomous navigation in crowded, human-centric environments. The key insight is that encoding spatial influence from nearby agents via a novel spatial attention mechanism—designed to be more parameter-efficient, interpretable, and less assumption-dependent than prior spatial attentions—allows better capture of local social interactions that drive pedestrian motion. The method, called SCAN, jointly predicts multiple socially-acceptable future trajectories for all pedestrians by using this spatial context attentive network to weight neighbors’ influences and generate multimodal trajectory hypotheses. Experiments on multiple datasets show SCAN yields improved accuracy in intent prediction compared to state-of-the-art trajectory prediction approaches.

The paper tackles shortcomings in Composed Image Retrieval (CoIR), namely the scarcity and quality issues of existing datasets and the challenge of effectively fusing image and text queries. Its key insight is that scaling dataset size and diagnosing modality redundancy can substantially boost CoIR performance and that early cross-attention fusion with an auxiliary task yields stronger representations. To that end the authors introduce LaSCo, a new CoIR dataset an order of magnitude larger than prior sets, propose an analysis method to detect when image or text modalities are redundant or necessary in queries, and present CASE (Cross-Attention driven Shift Encoder), a baseline that fuses modalities early via cross-attention and uses an auxiliary training objective. Pretraining on LaSCo and using CASE leads to significant gains, including improved zero-shot performance and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like FashionIQ and CIRR.

args.text: We propose Joint Hyperparameter Entropy Search (JHES), an information-theoretic acquisition that maximizes the expected reduction in entropy of the joint distribution over the optimizer (x*, y*) and GP hyperparameters, so early queries both localize the optimum and rapidly calibrate the surrogate. Building on JES, we approximate this objective by sampling hyperparameters from the current hyperposterior, fantasizing observations, and reusing JES’s conditional updates, while leveraging fast GP posterior sampling to keep computational cost comparable. To balance model calibration and pure optimization, we adaptively anneal the weight on the hyperparameter-entropy term according to its remaining uncertainty, yielding decisions that first learn hyperparameters when needed and then concentrate on the optimum. result.text: TensorNet addresses the challenge of building computationally efficient, O(3)-equivariant neural networks for learning molecular potentials and related vector/tensor properties. The key insight is that using Cartesian tensor atomic embeddings plus matrix-product feature mixing, combined with an economical decomposition into rotation-group irreducible components, lets the model treat scalars, vectors, and higher-order tensors separately and more simply than high-rank spherical-tensor approaches. result.text: The paper tackles feature-based knowledge distillation, where conventional approaches match a single teacher layer to a single student layer and can fail to transfer the teacher’s intact representation. The key insight is that forcing multiple student sub-representations to jointly approximate the teacher’s representation (an N-to-one matching) preserves more teacher information and yields stronger supervision while adding no inference cost. Methodologically, they insert a lightweight two-layer linear Feature Transform (FT) after the student’s last convolution: the first linear layer expands the student feature channels by a factor N, the expanded vector is split into N non-overlapping segments that are each matched to the teacher’s feature, and the second linear layer contracts back to the original dimensionality so the whole module can be merged into the following fully connected layer at inference; this simple training-time trick improves accuracy across several vision models and ImageNet.

A learned intervention policy selects minimal cross-modal edits—e.g., swapping comments among semantically similar posts, substituting visually equivalent frames, or masking modality-specific cues—and the detection score is the stability gap of the prediction under these counterfactuals; truthful items remain invariant, while fabrications that hinge on cross-modal inconsistencies flip, yielding compact, human-interpretable rationales. result.text: BayesDAG addresses Bayesian causal discovery: inferring posterior distributions over Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and associated structural functions from observational data, a task made difficult by the combinatorial DAG space and nonlinear relationships. The key insight is a novel equivalence between permutation-based DAG representations and adjacency-based formulations that permits applying relaxed, differentiable gradient estimators over permutations so that one can perform gradient-based posterior sampling without relying on DAG regularizers that fail to guarantee acyclicity. The method combines stochastic-gradient MCMC for sampling permutation matrices (thus directly sampling DAGs) with variational inference for function parameters, enabling joint, scalable posterior inference of both graph structure and nonlinear functions for linear and nonlinear causal models. Empirically, this gradient-based MCMC+VI framework yields more accurate and principled uncertainty-aware causal discovery than prior permutation- or relaxation-only approaches on synthetic and real datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of autonomous exploration and navigation in environments where geometric maps alone are insufficient—because of dynamic objects and semantic hazards—by combining learned scene understanding with traditional planners. Its key insight is that a learned spatial affordance map, trained via self-supervised interaction, can capture navigability and semantic constraints in a way that complements geometric planners, improving robustness and interpretability. The method trains an agent in VizDoom to predict affordance maps from observations gathered through active exploration, and integrates those maps with conventional SLAM-style planners to guide both exploration and pathfinding. Evaluations on large-scale, randomly generated maps with dynamic actors and hazards show that augmenting planners with learned affordances yields significant performance gains in navigation and exploration tasks.

args.text: We propose telemetry-conditioned GFlowNets for geo-distributed, heterogeneous model-parallel training that maintain an anytime, diverse portfolio of tasklet-to-device placements and pipeline schedules. The GFlowNet samples schedules with probabilities proportional to a robust latency–throughput objective conditioned on real-time bandwidth/latency and queueing telemetry, while an exact placement/pipeline feasibility layer prunes invalid assignments. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of generating high-quality synthetic tabular data that must handle heterogeneous field types and missing values while providing strong privacy-utility tradeoffs. The key insight is that a masked-transformer architecture with tailored masking strategies can natively represent mixed-type columns, model dependencies between fields, and impute or generate missing entries, yielding better sample fidelity and privacy behavior than existing autoregressive or ad-hoc tabular generators. The method, TabMT, adapts masked-transformer blocks and introduces improved masking schemes and training protocols specifically for tabular structures, enabling conditional and unconditional sampling, native missing-value handling, and scalable training across very small to very large tables; empirical evaluation shows state-of-the-art generation quality and superior privacy-utility tradeoffs.

result.text: The paper addresses whether permutation invariance lets one linearly interpolate between SGD solutions without encountering performance barriers, and identifies why existing neuron alignment methods fail: interpolated networks undergo "variance collapse," where activation variances shrink and degrade performance. The key insight is that this collapse, not misalignment alone, prevents low-barrier connectivity, and it can be remedied by re-scaling activations after permutation so that interpolated preactivations recover appropriate variances. The authors introduce REPAIR, which renormalizes permuted preactivations when constructing linear interpolations between matched neurons, and show empirically across widths, depths, and normalization types that applying REPAIR atop alignment methods dramatically reduces interpolation barriers (e.g., 74% for ResNet50 on ImageNet, 90% for ResNet18 on CIFAR10).
